maintopic: EXCHANGE OF NOTES SETTING OUT RECIPROCAL ARRANGEMENTS BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED STATES

speechtext:
Right Hon. W L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, I should like to lay on the table of the house copies in English and French of an exchange of notes with the United States setting forth an agreement on compulsory military service.
41561-114$
There are three notes. There is the note of March 30 from Mr. Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State, to the Canadian Minister in Washington; the note of April 6, No. 222, from the Canadian Minister in Washington to the Acting Secretary of State, and the note of April 8 from the Acting Secretary of State to Mr. Wrong, charge d'affaires in Washington.
The United States Selective Training and Service Act, when it was passed in the summer of 1940 applied only to United States citizens, and to aliens who had declared their intention of becoming United States citizens. The act was amended in December, 1941, after the entry of the United States into the war. One of the amendments which was then passed provided for the conscription of Canadians and of nationals of other co-belligerent countries who were resident in the United States, and who had not declared their intention of becoming United States citizens.
Thus, by last December all Canadians residing in the United States became subject to compulsory service on the same basis as the United States citizens. Subsequent to the passage of this legislation the United States informed us that they would be willing to permit some of these Canadians to elect to serve in the armed forces of Canada, in lieu of service in the armed forces of the United States. The United States offer applied to non-declarant Canadians-that is to say, to Canadians who had not declared their intention of becoming United States citizens. We gladly accepted this offer, since we agreed with the United States that the united war effort of our countries would be strengthened if Canadians in the United States who had not yet given evidence of their desire to make the United States their permanent home were given an opportunity to fight in the armed forces of their own country and under their own flag, instead of fighting in the armed forces of the United States.
The agreement is reciprocal in every respect. If United States citizens, in Canada should in future be made liable to compulsory military service in the Canadian armed forces they will be given exactly the same privileges as Canadians in the United States are being given by the United States government.
The United States government has also, by the exchange of notes, declared that it is agreeable to the Canadian government imposing on United States citizens residing in Canada a liability to compulsory military service.
It might be a convenience to hon. members if this exchange of notes were printed in the Votes and Proceedings of the house. They will be printed a little later in a series of
Pacific War Council
documents published by the Department of External Affairs, but it may be some time before that series is published.

subtopic: MEETINGS IN WASHINGTON-CANADIAN REPRESENTATION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MEETINGS IN WASHINGTON-CANADIAN REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he will make a statement at an early date concerning the Pacific council which was set up at Washington subsequent to the adjournment of this house on March 27.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MEETINGS IN WASHINGTON-CANADIAN REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the only
statement that I would be at liberty to make is one which I think I might make immediately. As my hon. friend knows, the Pacific war council was set up about three weeks ago. The meeting which was held on Wednesday of last week, and which I was invited by the President to attend, was the third meeting the council has held. The meeting of the war council was presided over by the President, and its proceedings were similar to the proceedings of a cabinet. I would not be at liberty myself to state what subjects were discussed or what conclusions were reached; any statement to be given out with respect to the proceedings of the council would be given out by the President. I understand that no announcement has been made of that particular day's proceedings or of the proceedings of the two previous meetings of the council.
The discussions, as would be obvious, related to war matters pertaining to the Pacific. No public intimation could be given of what was discussed because anything given to the public would be given equally to the enemy. At

the meeting which I attended there were present Sir Ronald Campbell, minister for the United Kingdom; Mr. Loudon, minister in the United States representing the Netherlands; Doctor Soong, representing China; Doctor Evatt, Minister for Foreign Affairs of Australia, who represented Australia, and the Hon. Mr. Nash, representing New Zealand.
I understand that meetings of the council will be held more or less regularly every week.
I believe it will be in the interests of the proceedings of the council that for the most part the same persons should represent the different countries at the respective meetings in order that they may be more familiar with the matters being discussed. I do not know that there is more that I can say at the moment, unless my hon. friend has some specific question to ask.

subtopic: MEETINGS IN WASHINGTON-CANADIAN REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Who will be representing
Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MEETINGS IN WASHINGTON-CANADIAN REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Our minister at Washington, Mr. Leighton McCarthy, will represent Canada at the meetings. Mr. McCarthy was not in Washington at the time of the first meeting. Mr. Hume Wrong, the counsellor of the legation, represented Canada on that occasion. At the second meeting Mr. McCarthy represented Canada. For reasons that will be obvious it has not been thought advisable that more than one person representing any country should be present at a meeting. If there were more than one representative of any country present, it might create embarrassment with respect to the representation of some of the other countries.

subtopic: MEETINGS IN WASHINGTON-CANADIAN REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I follow up that question? As the other dominions and countries are represented on the council by men who have had experience in the government of their country, does not the Prime Minister think that Canada should be represented by someone other than a high commissioner, someone who has had experience in the government of this country, a man of ministerial status?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MEETINGS IN WASHINGTON-CANADIAN REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Canada has not a high commissioner at Washington, but is represented by the Canadian minister to Washington.
I would say, as regards the present minister to Washington, that, as my hon. friend is no doubt aware, Mr. McCarthy was for many years a foremost member of this House of Commons. While he has not been a member of the government of Canada he has had wide parliamentary experience. Canada is exceedingly fortunate in having one of Mr. McCarthy's exceptional attainments to represent our country at Washington and in having

P/ie Plebiscite
him represent Canada at the meetings of the Pacific war council. I would also say that I think Mr. Hume Wrong, while he has not been in parliament, has had exceptional experience in diplomatic work in different countries and is exceedingly well qualified to represent Canada on any board or council such as the Pacific council. I would not feel that previous cabinet experience would necessarily be an essential qualification. It no doubt would be helpful inasmuch as the proceedings of the Pacific war council are carried on very much as proceedings would be in any cabinet. The personal qualifications of the representative would count for a great deal, I think, in respect of the effectiveness of his service.

subtopic: MEETINGS IN WASHINGTON-CANADIAN REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Prime Minister a further question? What relation has the Pacific conference which was established in London a month ago, representing certain countries, with Canada excepted, to the Pacific council at Washington, with Canada included? Will the London conference have to report to the Washington council, and will there have to be an exchange of notes before we can have any defence in the Pacific? What is the relation between the body in London and the one in Washington?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MEETINGS IN WASHINGTON-CANADIAN REPRESENTATION
speechtext: My hon. friend will recall I had some difficulty, when I was asked at an earlier stage of the session a question with respect to a Pacific war council in Washington, to say whether Canada would be represented on that council. My difficulty arose from the fact that a Pacific war council was formed in London, England, in the first instance, and at that time it was not certain whether a Pacific war council would ultimately be also formed in Washington. The council which was first set up in 'London was a gathering of the representatives of certain Pacific countries which were immediately involved in the operations in the southeast Pacific, brought together at the instance of the Prime Minister of Great Britain. At the present time provision has been made for the meeting from time to time in London of this counterpart of the Pacific council which meets ini Washington. Canada will continue to be represented on that body by the high commissioner. For the present it has been thought advisable to have the council dealing with Pacific affairs meet regularly in Washington rather than in London. The whole matter of the study of conditions in the Pacific has had to take shape more or less in accordance with the manner in which events have helped to shape it.

subtopic: MEETINGS IN WASHINGTON-CANADIAN REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Will not the London conference have to report to Washington first?
And in the meantime Japan may take action in the Pacific, as we have lost control of the sea in the Pacific.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MEETINGS IN WASHINGTON-CANADIAN REPRESENTATION
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, there is a combined strategy with which certain of the heads of the defence forces are concerned in London and also in Washington, and communications pass continuously between the two. There are bodies which exist alike in London and in Washington which have to do with questions that arise out of decisions with respect to strategy; but the fact that one exists in the one country and the other in the other does not mean that either is subordinate to the other. It is part of the arrangement under which the present war is being carried on, on behalf of the United Nations and which recognizes at the head as the combined command, the Prime Minister of Great Britain and the President of the United States.

subtopic: MEETINGS IN WASHINGTON-CANADIAN REPRESENTATION
speechtext: In other words, we are to depend on Washington instead of London for defence in the Pacific.

maintopic: QUESTION AS TO SPECIAL GASOLINE RATION ON VOTING DAY

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Mr. G. A. McLEA'N (Simcoe East): I should like to ask the Minister of Munitions and Supply if it is the intention to 'have a special ration of gasoline issued for the plebiscite day?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO SPECIAL GASOLINE RATION ON VOTING DAY
speechtext:
Consideration has been given to this matter. Is is obvious, to all those who are familiar with the situation, that to make any special provision for gasoline for the plebiscite day is quite impossible. The only notice which has appeared in the press on this matter was a quotation from a speech of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson). Repercussions from the oil administrator of the United States followed immediately; I believe the oil controller had a telephone message at noon next day.
The situation is that Canada is very heavily dependent upon the United States, not only for petroleum, but for the transportation of petroleum. All of us who read the newspapers know that the sinking of tankers has been extremely heavy, and our Canadian fleet has suffered along with the rest. Under these circumstances I think it would be a negation of the purpose of the plebiscite to provide additional gasoline for bringing out the vote.
When speaking in my own riding, I asked my constituents to give as freely of -their gasoline as they were giving of their time. I got a very favourable response. I believe

that all those who have an appreciation of the importance of the plebiscite will gladly provide the gasoline required, not only to convey themselves to the poll, but also to assist others who would be unable otherwise to cast their votes.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO SPECIAL GASOLINE RATION ON VOTING DAY
speechtext: I regret the decision. I hope that the expectation of the minister with respect to the voluntary surrender of coupons for use on plebiscite day will be met. I made -the announcement to which he refers as having had repercussions, simply upon a message which I received from one of the minister's secretaries that the matter was under consideration: that was as far as I ever went. I was hopeful that a formula might be adopted which would give some leeway in the use of gasoline on that day, because in the rural -parts of the country it is going to be very difficult to get gasoline for the transportation of voters to -the polls, and I do not think that they will walk.

subtopic: SHIPBUILDING-STRIKES AT MIDLAND AND KINGSTON

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: SHIPBUILDING-STRIKES AT MIDLAND AND KINGSTON
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour as a result of two telegrams I have received this morning from the Midland shipyards. First, will the minister tell us what is the cause of the dispute at the shipbuilding plants in Midland and Kingston; and, second, what action- is being taken to settle it?

subtopic: SHIPBUILDING-STRIKES AT MIDLAND AND KINGSTON
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman did not give me any notice .of the question. In the first place, the strike at Midland was called without any knowledge of the department; it was called because a man was demoted and then laid off. A conciliation officer was sent in there, and an agreement was arrived at with the company that the man would be given his job back, and that the men could return to work without discrimination. It was pointed out to them prior to that that the strike was illegal. Following that they placed further demands before the company. The department took the position it always takes in the case of an illegal strike: first of all the men must return to work. The next step was the calling of a sympathetic strike at Kingston in support of the Midland workers who went on strike because this or man was laid off. I would say this about Kingston: they had an agreement with the company under which all disputes would be submitted to a tribunal of employers and em-

Canadian Army
ployees. Notwithstanding that, and the fact that they were told it was illegal to strike, they went on strike. Now the position taken by the department is that the question is no longer one for us to deal with; it is a question for the Department of Justice. I would like to say this, though: it would be just too bad if the men who go down to the sea in ships, in corvettes, went on strike because a man was demoted.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF HON. FRANK LANGSTONE AS HIGH COMMISSIONER IN CANADA

speechtext:
The house will be pleased, I am sure, to know that this morning, at Wellington, the Prime Minister of New Zealand announced that the Hon. Frank Langstone has been appointed to represent New Zealand in Canada as high commissioner in this country. Mr. Langstone has had an important public career, having served in the House of Representatives of New Zealand, also having been Minister of Lands and Native Affairs in his own country. With Mr. Langstone's appointment we will now have in Ottawa high commissioners from all the self-governing parts of the British empire, just as Canada is represented in all parts of the British empire by our high commissioners.

subtopic: EMBARKATION INCIDENT AT AN EASTERN CANADIAN PORT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: EMBARKATION INCIDENT AT AN EASTERN CANADIAN PORT
speechtext:
I should like to address a question to the Minister of National Defence. A bulletin was posted to-day in front of a local newspaper office to the effect that 400 soldiers left a ship at an eastern Canadian port, and that 135 of those soldiers had missed the vessel when it sailed. Would the minister care to make a statement to the house about this occurrence? If that bulletin was posted following a statement issued by the Minister of
National Defence, would he tell us why a statement is issued to the public before the members of this house are informed of the occurrence?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: EMBARKATION INCIDENT AT AN EASTERN CANADIAN PORT
speechtext: Answering the last question first, Mr. Speaker, I do not agree that each statement issued from the Department of National Defence must necessarily be communicated first to the House of Commons. The statement was issued as soon as it was possible to issue it after the safe arrival of that particular convoy, and it was given to the press. As a matter of fact it was issued this morning and communicated to the press for the afternoon papers. I know it has been suggested here from time to time that no statements should be made to the press unless they have first been made here.

subtopic: EMBARKATION INCIDENT AT AN EASTERN CANADIAN PORT
speechtext: No-on matters of policy, not factual matters.

subtopic: EMBARKATION INCIDENT AT AN EASTERN CANADIAN PORT
speechtext:
I am glad to hear my hon. friend say that, because I am sure the House of Commons is not to be regarded as a bulletin board, where a department has to make statements in the house in regard to matters of detail or administration which are ordinarily published in the papers. That is the answer to my hon. friend's second question.
Answering the first question, I am sorry I have not before me at the moment the statement which was issued to the press. Briefly, about 400 men walked off the ship at Halifax at the time of embarkation, and about 135 had not returned or did not get back to the pier in time to be embarked. The situation, as set out in the statement, was that the ship arrived very much later than she was expected. The time for disembarking those who were on the ship, for loading provisions-and by the way, they were to load eight weeks' provisions plus an additional twelve days' provisions-for cleaning the ship and for loading personnel to go on the ship, was cut to about half of the normal time. The result was some confusion, and some dissatisfaction, particularly with the condition of the ship and the rations. A special party was put on to make conditions as livable and comfortable as possible and I think that every step possible was taken to make the situation as agreeable as it could be under the circumstances. But there is no doubt in my mind that the ship was not in as good condition as is normally the case with troop-ships. As a matter of fact, the embarkation officials examined the ship and, after their examination, determined that the number to be carried on it should be reduced by about 20 per cent from the number
Canadian Army

which had been carried on her inward voyage; and notwithstanding that, these men walked off the ship as a protest against conditions in connection with the ship itself and with regard to rations. Many of them came back. Some of them were rounded up. All but 135 sailed on the ship and of that number some came back voluntarily and some were rounded up. They got back to the ship too late. She was in the stream. She had weighed anchor and they were too late to go on board. Disciplinary action has been taken with regard to them. I have no doubt from the information I have received that they were led astray by a few ringleaders, and these ringleaders are being specially dealt with. It is obvious that the situation was such that their action could not be condoned. It was not a case where men could take the situation into their own hands, and it would be manifestly unfair to the vast proportion of the men who embarked on the ship and who are now safely overseas.
I read further from the statement which has just been handed to me.	Generally
speaking, those who disobeyed orders expressed their disappointment and regret when they got to the dock and found the ship had gone. They had been warned that the ship would sail but they believed they had time to go ashore for a final fling before embarking. Conditions on board troop-ships are often cramped and not too comfortable, but the tens of thousands of Canadian soldiers who have gone overseas have recognized how necessary it is to utilize all available shipping and have put up with whatever discomforts there were as part of the day's work.
The difficulties were increased by the fact that the contingent which sailed on this ship was made up of no less than sixty-nine different reinforcing detachments and they therefore could not be organized and closely controlled in the same way as complete units would have been.
We are putting our views very clearly before the United Kingdom authorities in order to prevent a recurrence of conditions so far as transports are concerned. At the same time we are making certain changes in the embarkation and troop conducting system with particular reference to troops which are not in organized units. I can say definitely that corrective action is being taken. I am confident that there should be no excuse for a repetition of this isolated incident which in the absence of explanation might have reflected on the good name of Canadian soldiers.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF THE PRESENT WAR

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, April 20, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver Centre) -Mr. Vien in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to make provision for the settlement on the land of veterans of the present war, to prescribe the terms of such settlement and to grant a

Veterans' Land Act
measure of financial assistance to such settlers, and further for the appointment of a director, of officers and other employees in connection therewith.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF THE PRESENT WAR
speechtext:
In making his statement last night the minister said that the new settlement bill would provide for assistance to men who wish, to take up small holdings and who would be earning at least a portion of their income in some other way than by farming.
I wonder if he would amplify that statement. For example, will the bill cover those men who wish to take up an acre or two outside our cities or towns? In recent years there has been some movement in that direction and I think that if the bill is made broad enough to cover that particular class of soldier it might be very helpful in improving conditions which have existed in our cities throughout the depression years.
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Pensions and National Health): The answer is yes. The bill is much more flexible in that regard than the old Soldier Settlement Act, but it is intended to have possibly a qualifications committee set up to deal with small holdings and with the question whether men might be self-sustaining or whether there might be supplementary wages earned in the cities or small towns.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF THE PRESENT WAR
speechtext: Is it intended to cover only the exceptional case, or will there be many thousands of such cases?

speechtext: It is contemplated as a definite policy under the proposed bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF THE PRESENT WAR

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF THE PRESENT WAR
speechtext: If he had employment, that would be a condition precedent.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF THE PRESENT WAR
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. HANSON (York-SunbupO: What are the buttresses to which the minister has just referred as being prerequisite to assistance under this scheme?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF THE PRESENT WAR
speechtext: In regard to the small holdings, the buttress would be reasonable assurance of employment opportunity within a reasonable distance of the holding.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF THE PRESENT WAR
speechtext: Is it intended to have small holdings adjacent only to industrial areas, or will they also be established in places adjacent to the cities of western Canada?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF THE PRESENT WAR
speechtext: I understand it is the intention to have them in the vicinity of industrial areas where there would be reasonable assurance of employment opportunity.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF THE PRESENT WAR
speechtext: I regret that the exigencies of the occasion-I think that is a good phrase-compelled me to leave the chamber last evening before the minister had completed his statement.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF THE PRESENT WAR
speechtext: You were rendering very good service.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF THE PRESENT WAR
speechtext:
I hope so;
I am not always the best judge of my own efforts. I should like to express my thanks to the minister for the courtesy he extended to me in sending some time ago a review of the remarks which he made last night. I am interested in this question of land settlement. I am not at all sure that it will be a success;
I have grave doubts, for various reasons. I am not going to pour cold water on the scheme; I hope it may be a success. But undoubtedly its success or failure will depend in large measure on the management, the character of the men who undertake obligations under the scheme, and the direction given to the men.
One of the first requisites for a land settlement scheme in respect of farming is that the applicant must have a genuine love of the soil. It is no good to put a man on a farm unless his heart is in it. Many of the men from the cities and towns in the old country who were brought out here under land settlement schemes had no knowledge of conditions in this country and had no real love of the soil. That I think is the first requisite for the successful operation of any scheme of this kind.
The second requisite is some knowledge of farming. I am speaking of those who will become genuine farmers. I want to impress upon the minister and upon his officials who are to operate this legislation, that a man cannot be put upon a farm and achieve success unless he has some knowledge of the work. The officials who are supervising should make very certain that the applicant has a knowledge of the vocation which he intends to attempt.
A third requisite is that no scheme of land settlement for farms should be undertaken with public funds unless the conditions are such that a man may have reasonable expectation of success. I know something about the soldier settlement scheme. It was started as a result of a public demand. Canada had vast
Veterans' Land Act

open spaces, large areas of crown land available for settlement. The scheme was meant to operate for the most part in western Canada where land was still available for settlement, and it was subject to conditions then existing which to my mind doomed it to failure almost from the beginning. I am not familiar with the situation in the west, but in the east there was failure because of inflated values. The minister referred to that last night. But that was not by any means the only cause of failure. One of the chief causes was the failure of the administrative staff-I do not remember who they were, and at the moment it is not important-to see to it that the proper farms were purchased.
One member I heard to-day discussing this matter said that on some of the farms sold to returned soldiers they could step from one stump to the other. I can recall farms in my own province where the returned soldier could almost leap from one rock-pile to the other; from the very beginning he could not hope to scratch a living out of the soil under the conditions that obtained. Therefore a very great deal depends upon the skill and ability and judgment of those who are administering the scheme. The success or failure of the scheme so far as land settlement is concerned will depend in large measure upon the ability of those administering it and their exercise of proper judgment.
An interesting question was raised last night by the hon. member for Lethbridge as to whether we required more farmers in this country. I have my own view. I have never thought that a nation like Canada could have too much agricultural production. If we do not produce we shall never get anywhere. In my own province the lack of success of farmers is due to lack of quality production. The farmers of New Brunswick are not producing enough to feed our own population. Yet in many respects their plight is pitiable. It is a sad admission to make, but I think it is true largely of the maritime provinces generally-
I could except Prince Edward Island, of course, because I believe in certain lines it produces enough to feed its people. But we have continuous!}' the spectacle of foodstuffs being brought in by the carload from Ontario', meat products especially. That should not be.
I am glad to be able to say there is a movement in that province now for greater meat production, sponsored I understand by the superintendent of the experimental station at Fredericton, who is very much alive to the situation. But the reason for the lack of production in New Brunswick is that for years farming in that province, and in various parts of the maritime provinces as well as elsewhere, has not been profitable.

Until it can be demonstrated that men can go on the land and make a reasonable living I do not think the scheme should be encouraged too much. What inducement is there to put a man on a farm in western Canada ito raise wheat? Let us take the classic case, because we hear more in this house about that than anything else. I do not think anyone should be encouraged to buy a wheat farm in western Canada under this scheme until conditions are different from what they are to-day. We might produce more dairy products in this country if we established the necessity for them, and dairy products are in very good demand at the moment. We should encourage the production of more wool. And by the way, without wanting to start a discussion I should like to put this query to the Minister of Finance. Why is it that under the price ceiling the price of wool has been fixed at 25 cents a pound while just across the line it is 41 cents, a difference of about 70 per cent?

I am going to leave it at that. There are various lines of agricultural endeavour which could be made profitable to the farmer if he were allowed to have a little free scope. I suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that it is his duty-and I think perhaps he is already aware of that, and has been endeavouring to give effect to it-to see that the agricultural producer in this country gets a fair return, having regard to all the circumstances, and the conditions which confront this nation to-day. I am sure he is not unmindful of the position and will not be derelict in his duty, in so far as he has the power to produce that result.
I could speak with respect to the potato farmers in my own province who operate at a loss three seasons out of four and who, in the fourth season when they have a chance to operate at a profit, are met by this ceiling. No floor, may I add, is put under them.

All these things work inequalities which are not conducive to settling the land or to greater production from the land. There are certain aspects of the scheme which are quite commendable, and there are certain others which I query: I have not lived on the land, but for forty years in my own constituency I have been very close to it. I believe I can say I have as much money invested in the land in my own community as any other individual in that community. At all times I have tried my utmost, and always with great difficulty, to keep people on the land.
When this scheme is crystallized into legislation and becomes operative, I suggest the greatest care should be exercised in its operation. Do not let us have any stampede of men to go on the land because of an attractive offer-and I do not deny that from a financial point of view the offer is attractive. The state is making a substantial contribution, to which I raise no objection. I am not objecting to anything which may be done for the reestablishment of returned soldiers. But the element of selectivity must be exercised. A man's own conception of bis abilities may not be the best one. A disinterested judgment by those who are competent to judge is essential. I hope there will be no great rush to buy land on which to settle farmers unless certain prerequisites are determined by the department.
I have tried to lay down only three of these prerequisites, and I believe they are sound. By the way, I notice this scheme is not to be administered by the minister. Perhaps he is to be congratulated upon getting out from under so far as the actual administration is concerned. I should hope that his colleague who is to administer the act, under a single director, will at least read my remarks, and perhaps act on them.
No one should be put on the land simply because he wants to be there. He must have a love of the soil and must know something about farming. Before he is allowed to go on the land there should be reasonable probability of his making a success. This country should not be buying land for men who will not succeed or who will not work. Let it be understood that the fact that the government is handling it is not the important factor. A man must be prepared to work, just as you and I have had to work, and as we will have to work for the rest of our days.
I wish this scheme well. I should like to see everything possible done for the reestablishment of the soldiers, but I certainly advise great caution. First I would say to the director: Beware of the land shark who will
sell you farms for a consideration. Eliminate them, if you can, and deal directly with the owner. One great defect in the last scheme was indicated by the fact that a soldier who was the son of a farmer would apply for land and would wind up by buying his father's farm. That must be avoided, at all costs. The soldier would get the farm, under the agreement; his father had the money, and the farm was sold to the government.

speechtext:
I desire to express my support of this resolution, and to say at the outset that I do not share the pessimism expressed by some hon. members. In my view a plan for soldier settlement on the land after the war is both desirable and in every way necessary, and is to the advantage not only of the returned soldiers but of Canada as a whole.
My remarks will deal chiefly with only one phase of the situation, namely, settlement in the area with which I am best acquainted and which is represented in this chamber by the hon. member for Cariboo and myself. Before dealing *with any particular aspect of the matter, however, I should like to make a few general observations.
I am quite well aware that there are many difficulties confronting any settlement scheme. There is no doubt that western Canada's landscape is strewn with the wreckage of settlement schemes which have failed. Following the last w'ar soldier settlement was not the success it might have been, but
179S
Veterans' Land Act

neither was it the great failure some hon. fnembers would have us believe. So far as western Canada is concerned I believe it will be found that the number of soldier settler failures compared favourably with the number of failures of ordinary settlers.
We have heard the argument that because the farmer of to-day cannot make a living it is useless to put more settlers on the land. In this argument there is of course some merit. But surely if we can predict anything we can predict that we are going to win this war, and that in that victory there will be something new which will mean a better day for agriculture. I believe this resolution is predicated on two things, the winning of the war and a new day for agriculture following that victory.
I agree with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) when he says that those who will be responsible for this legislation will have to exercise a tremendous amount of care. I was impressed by what he said about the type of man who should come under this legislation. I was struck particularly by his phrase " love of the soil ". I think that phrase embodies a principle that should be followed. I do not think it is sufficient that the returned man was on a farm before he went overseas. I do not think it is sufficient that a certain amount of training may be given. I agree that both these things are necessary, but there must be something more. There has to be what we might describe as a temper for farm life.
I should like to give the committee a few interesting figures from an analysis made by Professor Dawson and Professor Murchie of field studies in the Peace River country in the years 1929 and 1930. They examined some 332 farmers who were located on different types of farms. Some were in well-settled areas, others in the homestead areas, and others in the in-between areas. Of those 332 farmers, 28 per cent had worked only at farming while 72 per cent had been engaged in other pursuits. Of the 332, 81-6 per cent were born on farms and 18-4 per cent were born in towns or cities. Twenty-five per cent had no previous agricultural experience, while 75 per cent had had one or more years' agricultural experience. Of the 75 per cent who had had some agricultural experience, 50 per cent had had from one to nine years' farm training; 32 per cent had had training of from ten to nineteen years, and 18 per cent had had twenty years or more of training.
They examined twenty farmers who had the highest farm labour income. Of the twenty, five had been farmers all their lives and fifteen had spent some part of their lives 
in other gainful occupations. Then they examined twenty farmers who had the lowest farm labour income, and the same thing applied there; five of them had been farmers all their lives and fifteen had been engaged in other gainful occupations for part of their lives. Again they took the experienced farmers and of those in the highest group it was found that they had an average of nineteen years' farming experience, but those in the lowest group had had an average of twenty-one years' farming experience.
I give these figures in order to make this point: one cannot be dogmatic as to what qualifications or what attributes an applicant should possess. It is not enough to say that he must have been a farmer in the past, or that he must have farming experience. While that principle should be kept in mind, there is a greater principle; as the leader of the opposition has said, the applicant must have a love of the land; he must have a temper for farm life.
Another question is the initial capital that a soldier settler should have. We know that in the scheme following the last war he had an indebtedness amounting to 90 per cent, or in some cases 100 per cent, of the value of his property. Inflated values prevailed at that time. It is quite evident that one poor season would wipe out any equity in the property. From the statement of the minister I take it that under this scheme he will have an equity at the start of at least 50 per cent. That is the amount of equity which the mortgage companies require before granting a mortgage, and it is the amount of equity required by the Canadian farm loan board. It seems to me that in that regard he should be placed in a much more favourable position than the soldier settler after the last war.
The leader of the. opposition made reference to administration, and I do not think he stressed that point too strongly. There were weaknesses in the administration of the soldier settlement scheme following the last war, but personally I have a great deal of confidence that the present director of soldier settlement, Mr. Murchison, and the very able supervisors he has now-I am fairly well acquainted with these men in my own province-will make a success of this matter. They know their work, they know their settlers, and there is every reason to expect that they will make a success of it so far as administration is concerned.
I come now to a phase of the matter in which I am particularly interested, that is, the question of new land versus old land. I realize that of necessity most of the land acquired for these soldier settlers will be acquired from private owners. I suggest that

Veterans' Land Act
there are several disadvantages in that. One disadvantage is that you will be buying land from farmers who are now operating, thus putting them on the labour market or into the field as competitive purchasers of other land. However, there is another angle; you may be purchasing land from farmers who because of advanced years are no longer efficient producers. Such land purchases would be all to the good. A great deal of caution will have to be exercised in the purchase of land from private owners. The land may be marginal or submarginal land; it may be overrun with weeds or generally run down. The leader of the opposition emphasized another disadvantage. These purchases are likely to cause speculation in farm lands and raise the purchase price of these lands far above their productive value.
Coming from the Peace River district, I am naturally interested in the frontier. I feel that a large number of these returned soldiers will inevitably seek the frontier. History will Tepeat itself. The Peace River country was settled largely after the last war, and returned soldiers played a great part in the settlement of that country. Probably the majority of these men were not under the soldier settlement scheme, and to-day these soldiers form the backbone of the Peace River country. Between 4,000 and 5,000 of their sons have enlisted, out of a total population of some 60,000. I believe this constitutes a record for the dominion. These 4,000 or 5,000 young men are either overseas or serving in Canada, and every one of them is a salesman for the Peace River country. When they come back they will desire to settle on the land, and they will bring a lot of friends with them.
The building of the Alaska highway is directing new attention to the Peace River country. A large number of United States soldiers are working on that highway and have passed through this country. I am told that a great many of them are keenly interested in settling in the Peace River country after the war. If we are not going to settle this vacant land with our own soldiers, I do not see how in the world we can prevent a large number of returned United States veterans from going there and taking up land. There is in this country the only agricultural frontier remaining unsettled in Canada.
The report of the Rowell-Sirois commission estimates that there are still available 16,000,000 acres of arable land in western Canada, the greater part of it in the Peace River country. This may be an underestimate, but it is probably pretty nearly correct. That land is in part first-class prairie soil, and first-class or second-class wooded soils
which will require clearing. The colony at Tupper Creek has shown that the only way to clear that wooded soil is by mechanical equipment, with which you can clear one or two hundred acres at a time, and that is what will have to be done if that land is to be made available for settlement. This land is not particularly adapted to the growing of wheat, but it is particularly adapted to mixed farming.
There is available in the Peace River country an area which can take care of a large number of returned soldier settlers. I feel that it could take care of all the 25,000 soldier settlers which this measure contemplates, and I think the minister and the department would be very well advised to make this Peace River country the spearhead of their whole settlement policy. You must have some spearhead which will sell this policy not only to the returned men but to the people of Canada. So far as the Peace River country is concerned that territory has already through the years been sold to the people. It has been sold to this house since the days of Hon. Frank Oliver, who spoke here on its behalf. It has been sold to this house by Mr. Kennedy, a former member, and by Mr. Pelletier, my immediate predecessor, representing the constituency of Peace River. It has been sold to this house by other members such as the member for Cariboo, the member for Athabaska, the member for Skeena, the member for Chambly-Rouville, the member for Vancouver-Burrard, the member for New Westminster, and more recently by the member for Davenport, who visited the Peace River country last summer. He came, he saw, he was conquered, and he is coming back again. None of the things which these members have told this house of the Peace River country in times past has been an exaggeration. Here are some of the things which the Minister of Pensions and National Health said about that territory. He referred to it as "that Peace River empire"- "that marvellous territory, tremendously rich in resources"-"the last great undeveloped portion of this dominion, that splendid north-land"-"what is in very essence and very truth a valuable empire in itself." And the Prime Minister has referred to it in these words: "The Peace River country is amongst the richest in Canada"-"a great tract of land crying out for development."
It has the soil, the climate and the sunlight. Nine times in the last fifteen years the Peace River country has brought the wheat championship to Canada. No other agricultural area in Canada has so many hours of sunlight during the growing season as the
Veterans' Land Act

Peace River country, and spring comes earlier there than in any other part of western Canada except in the most southerly part of southern Alberta.
I feel, Mr. Chairman, that the day of haphazard planning of settlement in Canada has passed, or should have passed, and if the present scheme is to be a success it must be most carefully and thoroughly planned. There is no area in Canada where the foundation has been better laid for planned settlement than in the Peace River country Exhaustive soil surveys have been made of that territory by the province of Alberta, by Doctor Wyatt. Studies of settlement conditions in the area were made in 1929 and 1930 by Doctor W. A. McIntosh of Queen's university, by Professor C. A. Dawson of McGill, and by Professor R. W. Murchie of the university of Minnesota. These studies are all contained in a volume entitled "The Peace River Country" in Canadian Frontiers of Settlement. It is an exhaustive study of settlement and plans for settlement of that area. Much similar work has also been done by the experimental farm and illustration stations, and there has been the work of the soldier settlement board itself and of district agriculturists, as well as the many studies made by the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National Railways. Of late years we have had in the constituency represented by the hon. member for Cariboo the Sudeten colony, whose experiences have brought out information which should be very useful to the minister and the department in any settlement scheme of this kind.
Such a scheme as this, Mr. Chairman, involves a good deal more than just putting the soldier settler on the land and then telling him to root, hog, or die. It means in the Peace River country a great deal more than that if the soldier is to be settled on new land. It means the building up of auxiliary services; it means settling the soldier conveniently to railway and other facilities if he is to have a chance to make good in a real way. He must have contact with all the social services which are required. The settlement of new communities of itself creates, openings for other returned soldiers in a business and professional way. Any such new settlement also means the purchase of equipment, which in turn gives employment to returned soldiers in other parts of the country. And particularly new settlement means this, that you are getting the utmost in value for what you put out.
So far as the Peace River country is concerned, soldier settlement in that area must also mean the development of adjacent areas. 
One such area is now being developed by the Alaska highway. It would mean the development also of such areas as the Yellow Knife mining field and the -rich mining areas lying west of the Rocky mountains in the constituency of Cariboo. It would mean an outlet to the Pacific coast. It would mean all these things and more. I feel very strongly, sir, that there should be vision in any plans made in this connection, and that the Alaska highway, that magnificent and gigantic undertaking, should be a symbol of the scope of the development which will take place in that area.
Settlement means something more so far as the Peace River country is concerned. It means transportation. This has been clearly established in the past, and it is just as clear to-day. In that connection I should like to quote what Sir Edward Beatty said on September 27, 1937, on his return to Edmonton after visiting the Peace River country. I have been in communication with him recently and he tells me that he is still of the opinion that he expressed in these words in 1937:
That north country needs a settlement plan and needs it quickly, and together with that there should be a programme of rail development.
The Peace River district impressed me most favourably. But its one major need still is that of increased settlement. I am confident that the country could absorb at least twice the population it now bears.
I certainly intend to suggest to the federal government that it embark on a broad policy of settlement for the north. Extension of rail facilities should go hand in hand with colonization. That is something that should be axiomatic.
The Peace River country definitely needs more people, and the sooner it gets them, the sooner will an elaborate programme of rail development become feasible and imperative.
That territory is served by the Northern Alberta railway, which was incorporated by this parliament in 1929. The act of incorporation sets out certain rail extensions which the Northern Alberta railway was empowered to build. One of these extensions was from Grimshaw to the northern boundary of the province; another was from Spirit River to a point in British Columbia; another one was from Hines Creek to Fort St. John.
I quite agree that you cannot ask the railways to go in at this time for a programme of railway development. But, as my final thought, I certainly would like to urge that there should be a railway extension from Hines Creek to Fort St. John. It would open up an area which, according to the soil analyses of Doctor Wyatt, contains something like two million acres of the best arable land to be found in western Canada. More than

Veterans' Land Act
that, Fort St. John is the southern terminus of the Alaska highway. That point can now be reached only by a highway which crosses the Peace river by ferry. Surely, with the United States government putting up the money for that Alaska highway, the least that Canada can do is to make Fort St. John readily accessible by rail. I do not know whether the United States engineers have asked for that or not. They may be timid about suggesting to this government what railway extensions should be made; but, seeing that they are taking the responsibility of building the road, I believe our government should inquire of them whether such a railway extension would be of benefit to them. I am certain that the answer would be that such an extension would be of immense service.
That is all I have to say to-day. I wish only to repeat that I am most strongly in favour of the principle of this resolution. I urge that the legislation following it be put forward with vision, with wisdom, and with courage.

I wish to congratulate the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Sissons) upon the fine description he has given of the Peace River country. I hope, however, that the minister, and the director-whoever he may be-will not be so strongly impressed by the hon. member's eloquence that all the money to'be expended and all the soldiers to be settled under this scheme will be placed in the Peace River district. After all, good opportunities for soldier settlement exist in other parts of Canada, and places where they have just as good an opportunity to be successful as in the Peace River district, however fine that district may be.
I am in favour of a soldier settlement scheme of this nature. The minister has had the advantage of reviewing the last act and profiting by the errors which were made in the drafting of it and in its provisions. I have no doubt that the director, whoever he may be, when the time comes will have the same advantage of profiting by a study of the weaknesses in the administration of that act. I am not one of those who think that that measure and the administration of it were altogether a failure. Undoubtedly there were individual cases, indeed too many of them, which were not successful. But there is this to be considered, that the soldier who settled on the land some twenty-odd years ago under the former scheme was handicapped in a way which the present soldier may not be. Land values at that time were exceedingly high; since that time there has been a constant lessening of values until they have now reached a very low level indeed. It seems to
me that land can be purchased at the present time at a price which will give the present-day soldier much greater advantages than he had under the last scheme.
I fully agree with the leader of the opposition that two or three things are essential if this scheme is to be a success. First, we must have the right type of man to go on the land. Certain types are not cut out to be farmers. There are those who have not the proper qualifications for farming, just as there are men who have not the necessary qualifications for other callings. It seems to me that in large measure the success of the project will depend upon the director who selects these men. He will have an obligation difficult to discharge, and will likely make mistakes at one time or another.
The success of the scheme depends also upon the administration of the act. I am glad to say that I think the terms are very liberal indeed. The encumbrance on a farm should not be too heavy; in fact there was a saying among the older farmers that it should not exceed 50 per cent of the actual value of the farm if the farmer is to have any reasonable prospect of getting out of debt during his lifetime. That is as true to-day as it was in days gone by. There are, of course, always exceptions to a rule, but there have been altogether too many cases where the encumbrance was too high for the farmer to discharge during a normal lifetime.
I have already said that when the former act was brought into effect farm prices were too high and farms were purchased at too high a price. At the present time, it seems to me, that difficulty will not be encountered.
I am sorry that I have not had the privilege of studying as closely as I would have liked, what the minister said last evening. One thing I noticed is that the ceiling of expenditure is to be $4,800, of which $3,600 may be expended on the farm itself and the buildings, and $1,200 for equipment.

I wish to point out three or four principles in connection with this resolution. In the first place, it is not expedient at the present time to introduce such a measure. How does it come about that because we have a plebiscite next Monday these measures are being brought down at the present time when they are not primary or expedient? The result is that the questions which are of primary importance, questions having to do with the prosecution of the war, we are not allowed to discuss at all. How many soldiers overseas at the present time will want to go on the land when they return? In the first place the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) has announced a very extensive exemption from military service of farmers and their sons, and all that kind of thing. We have to be guided by experience in an important matter like this, and from the unhappy experience of the soldiers in the last war-the experience with regard to veterans going on the land-I am persuaded that at this time, until the war is won, the principle of this resolution is all wrong. I suggest that we should be very slow to adopt it, especially at a time like this. We all know what happened after the last war. I know a great many farmers who went on the land in Ontario to making a living, but because of lack of foresight, vision and efficiency what became of these men after the last war? They had to put up with unemployment, misery, want and greater and greater poverty and have their homes broken up, notwithstanding all the protective measures which the government gave them, including the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, which was a measure for the benefit of farmers and soldiers who went on the land.
Let me point out one or two features of this particular problem. In the first place, I think it is all moonshine at a time like this. It is not expedient to introduce this measure at this stage. I repeat, all this planning is nothing but moonshine when at this very hour Britain and Canada are fighting for their very lives, with the enemy at Canada's front and back doors. They kept on talking like this all last fall in Washington about what they were going to do after the war, until Pearl Harbour came. I suggest that the wreckage will be so great after the war that there will be little to salvage, especially for the men who have gone to the front. With all the exemptions that I have indicated, I know that there are a good many men who do not want to go on the land. A large majority of the recruits are from the industrial centres in our cities and towns and they will not be booted about the country as the men were who came home after the last

war. They will not be booted about by a lot of stay-at-homes advising them to go on the land, when farmers' sons themselves are going into munitions plants making six, seven, eight and sometimes nine dollars a day with overtime, while these brave men are risking their lives on land, on sea and in the air to protect us, and doing it for $1.30 a day. That is what they are doing, and yet their dependents are denied a cost of living bonus. Some civilians in the civil service get $175 a month and the Minister of Finance rises in the house and gives people of that class a cost of living bonus, while next door is a soldier's wife with four or five children. While that breadwinner is over in England or on the seven seas fighting the battles of the country, how is he treated? How are his dependents treated? He is refused a cost of living bonus although his rent, groceries and everything else are the same as those of his neighbour who does not go overseas to fight. Do you think that these soldiers who have been fighting our battle will put up with this sort of thing as they did in the last war? I say no. It is the duty of the government first to win the war, to put first things first.
Regarding the expediency of introducing this measure, I would quote a couple of lines from something that Napoleon said in his correspondence. At a time like this when the enemy is at the door we are taking a plebiscite, and the government is bringing up secondary matters. This is the second day since we have come back and we are discussing only secondary matters; the chief issue before us, the war, is not being touched. In his Correspondence, No. 15212, Napoleon said that "by gambling with the lives of men you lose the confidence of the troops." That is what we are doing at the present time. We are gambling on the fact that we have had protection on land and sea and in the air through the mother country and we are gambling that the enemy will never invade our own country. We may have a rude awakening. We are therefore proposing all these secondary matters that could very well wait for a time, until the war is won.
War searches men and policies. In the first two years of the last war they were going on like this in Britain. They were considering politics and they made all kinds of mistakes, until in 1917 they decided that these domestic questions should wait until the war was won, otherwise you have the cart before the horse. The result was that at the end of 1916, with the dominions represented, an imperial war cabinet, proposed by Lord Milner, was formed, and it had a great effect in winning the war. It is unfortunate that that is not put into
effect now instead of measures like this, at a time like this, which lead nowhere. The people of this country want something done about the war first.
What about soldiers who were industrial workers in the cities? They do not know anything about farming; why are they not protected? I asked years ago for the protection of that class of worker under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. In the last war a great many did go on the land and suffered untold hardships. This way of dealing with this problem is all wrong. To the former minister of national war services I proposed a plan in 1936-38 by which these young people, who have now nearly all gone to the war but were then riding around the country on freight trains, should be given some measure of protection by which they could learn a trade, get clothing and lodging and pay, and get military training. One way the government can help large numbers of these returned soldiers is by adopting a large building and reconstruction policy near to and in cities. The proposal in 1935 was along that line. The government spent nearly $80,000,000 on reconstruction and housing. That would do as much as or far more for the soldiers at the front to-day who do not understand farming than such a measure as this. A man cannot learn to be a farmer in a day. You can learn to be a member of parliament in a day and talk about these secondary problems, but you cannot make a success of farming without some knowledge of it, no matter how much protection is given.
Another point is that a great many of these young men who went to the war were apprentices in some kind of industry. To ask them to give all that up and go on a farm is not feasible in all cases. In any event this should wait until the war is won. We are not yet mobilized for war in Canada. The mentality of the people of Canada is not a war mentality; that is plainly shown by the introduction of this resolution. The whole way of doing business here is an illustration of what Mr. Churchill spoke of as the enormous and unquestionable part humbug plays in the life of great people dwelling in a state of democratic freedom. He was referring to the bringing up of domestic matters that could well wait until after the war is won. I do not ask the government to wait that long. But I do say that if that is the form of protection soldiers in England and overseas are going to get when they come back home, telling them to go on the land, when their families have been treated the way they have been, being refused a cost of living bonus, they are made sick and tired.
Veterans' Land Act

I hope the government will get on with the war. They are marking time, waiting for something to happen to the plebiscite next Monday, but the enemy may be here before long.	It is not expedient to bring in a
measure like this now. We have had nothing but unbroken defeat for the last two and a half years; Norway, Dunkirk, Crete, Libya, Malaya, Hong Kong, Singapore, Burma; nothing but failure, and it is because we have failed to do our duty in the last twenty years; we have failed to rearm. I have every confidence in the minister; I admit that he has done much good war work in getting the army mechanized and in other matters. But I think these matters are secondary; we should have some total war effort before the minister goes into these problems, which can wait until after the war is won. We do not know yet who is going to own the country, let alone who is going to own the farms. The people who are protecting us are the men who have gone overseas.

speechtext:
The experiences of the
settlers under the old board have been such as to throw a wet blanket on this or any similar plan until we have in this country a different policy for agriculture. During the years I have been in this house we have argued persistently for a better agricultural policy, and to-day we are still waiting for that policy to be announced. I do not care what business a man may be in, farming or banking or anything else, so long as he is compelled to produce below cost there will be failure and failure and more failure, as we have had under the soldier settlement board and under all farming conditions.
The Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) told us last night that so many men had paid for their farms. I agree that a small percentage did pay for their farms, but the minister will have to agree that a number of them paid not with money earned on those

farms but because they had a little before, and a number of them who had money when they went on the soldier settlement plan are to-day without any. I know of several men who had pensions and sunk that money trying to pay soldiei settlement board loans, and to-day they are either on the road or threatened with eviction. That is not right. Until we have a different policy for agriculture there is no use trying to make a success of this or any other land policy. If a soldier settler is given free land and then is compelled to sell his product at below the cost of production, anyone will see that in the near future he will be on the road.
Last night the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), as reported at page 1777 of Hansard, suggested that inflation was the cause of failure of a number of men settled under the old soldier settlement board plan. I would say the government were responsible for the policy that existed at that time. If they did not control these matters in the interests of the common people instead of the privileged few, then the government must take the blame for the failure of these men. And if it was their responsibility to control the policy of the country, then it is their responsibility to make amends, even at this late day, for their thoughtlessness and carelessness in the past.
A number of what we might call arm-chair farmers have spoken on this question. Only a few moments ago one hon. member said it was necessary to have settlement in certain parts of the country so that railway facilities and that kind of thing could be built in. He even went so far as to quote Sir Edward Beatty. I believe the policy of the soldier settlement board and several other organizations in the past has been one, not of giving the people of Canada a living, but rather of building up Sir Edward Beatty's Canadian Pacific railway and other similar institutions. I do not believe it should be the policy of the government or the country to use any class for the purpose of building up railways or other companies. Rather the government's policy should be one of placing people in such a position that they may make a living. If the services and possibly the lives of our men overseas to-day have to be sacrificed so that others may make fat profits, then it is high time that some persons other than those in office to-day took over the reins of government.
I intend at a later stage to have something further to say with respect to soldier settlement on the land, but because it is out of order now I shall reserve it until the proper time.

PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF THE PRESENT WAR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as one
who took up land under the soldier settlement scheme after the last war, and one who has spent twenty-two years trying to pay for it, I believe I am familiar with this subject from the point of view of the settler. Much has been said to the effect -that the administration was not what it should have been. My experience, however, has been that the administration of soldier settlement was probably as fair as the administration of any other measure.
There were certain basic things which were wrong under the old act, and I am afraid they remain in the present one. I am not going to discuss in detail the provisions of the old act; I shall go into that more fully at a later time. I would point out, however, that under the old act there was no relationship between prices paid and values of products which had to be sold by the farmers later on. We bought land when it was worth a certain amount, when wheat was worth so much, and when cattle, horses and everything else were at certain prices. We are repeating the procedure to-day, only on a smaller scale.
To-day milch cows are selling at $85 each. Cream is selling at 32 cents or 33 cents a pound. What guarantee will the settler have when he buys his cattle that he will be able to dispose of his cream at 32 cents a pound?
Will he be in the same position as he was after the last war, when cream went down to 15 cents or 16 cents. After the war, what will prevent the Scandinavian countries from sending -their produce to the British markets? Shall we be able to compete with them? Under our present set-up, I do not think we shall.
The measure before us envisions a quarter-section as a farm. To-day in western Canada a quarter-section is not an economic unit to operate. The settlers who were able to pay for their land under the old act were those who were in a position to purchase other lands, so that they would have economic units to work. If we are to accept the quarter-section as a unit under this bill, then right from the start it is doomed to failure, because a quarter-section is not a satisfactory unit.
The tendency in agriculture to-day is toward specialization; we find it in every branch of the industry. If we go to the coast, we find poultry ranches with from 2,000 to 20,000 hens. Farms with only a hundred hens have no chance in competition. In my own constituency I know of men feeding a thousand hogs. The small farmer with only a couple of litters has no chance in that kind of competition. Especially is that true in reference to the grain farmers. What chance has a quarter-section of land to-day in competition with the large grain farms? It has no chance in the world; and if that is to be the basis under this measure, I can assure the committee that it is doomed to failure. In my own district I know that in the last two years seven quarter-section farms have been sold and absorbed into larger units. Most of those farmers were men who had twenty-five or thirty years' experience in farming, but they could not make it go. In many instances their farms were paid foT. How can we expect a young man who is green, as far as farming is concerned, to start in on a quarter-section farm and compete with a farmer who has one or two sections of land? It simply cannot be done.
One of the reasons why the old act was a failure, to a large extent, was that certain men who had not had experience and were unsuited to farming were placed on farms. That can be avoided this time. But the two remaining reasons cannot be avoided under this present measure, and I would seriously advise the government to think twice before making the quarter-section an economic unit. It has not proved successful in the past.
To-day in the United States certain schemes which I believe have seme chance of success
Veterans' Land Act

are in operation. Over there they have taken irrigated areas and have settled farmers on small acreages in those areas. Adjacent to them have been larger areas of land to be cultivated on a community basis. Those dry farms have been operated on a community basis, with the irrigated areas. Some such scheme might be set up in certain areas of the west, and I believe it would have a chance of success.
The small holdings suggested under the bill are a good thing, especially when they are set up adjacent to industrial areas where men can obtain part-time employment. That is a scheme which to a certain extent might be extended in western Canada. Around all our towns in the west we have certain developments along this line, where subdivisions are taken over by people who can obtain parttime employment either in the town or on the farms adjacent thereto. I believe that scheme could be developed in Canada for a certain type of individual who desires that kind of employment. But so far as accepting the quarter-section as a farming unit in western Canada is concerned, I doubt very much whether, in view of present-day competition from those who are specializing in various kinds of agriculture, it can be done.
