PROVISION FOR SETTLEMENT ON THE LAND OF VETERANS OF THE PRESENT WAR
speechtext:
First may I say that I am very glad indeed to note that the government is considering plans for the reestablishment of the returned men after the war. Because of the experience we had following the last war, I am not particularly enthusiastic about the bill that is before the committee. The figures presented last night by the minister himself regarding that experience are on record and show that out of some 25,000 settlers, the number now remaining on the land is approximately 8,000; those who have paid off their land number 2,700; those who
Veterans' Land Act

have sold their equity, 884; and the remainder, over 13.000, have abandoned the scheme either voluntarily or upon notice.
Yesterday from the veterans' association at Drumheller, from a committee of three, I received three pictures. They 'are large enough for most hon. members to see. The first one shows a soldier settlement home after twenty-two years-a shack so miserable that it is a wonder that any human being could inhabit it; yet it is inhabited by a family. Here is the second one, a little better than the first, and here is the third. I have seen so-called homes like these inhabited by soldier settlers across the prairies, and I am hoping that any scheme that we adopt will not be a scheme that will lend itself to this kind of thing.
I am thoroughly in agreement with what was said by the hon. member for Melfort who sat down a few moments ago, that if we are going to have a land settlement scheme for our soldiers we should make sure that the men who are to be settled on the land are settled in an economic unit and in proximity to a market or within reach of transportation facilities so that they can get to market and sell their produce. The economic unit, as he has said, as far as the prairies are concerned, is very much larger than most members of this house think. I am not going into the bulletins which have been issued by the university of Saskatchewan, and which we have quoted in this house from time to time, showing that the economic unit in many areas of the west to-day is at least a section, 640 acres, and that in some instances where the land is light, no sufficient living can be made by a family unless they have a full line of machinery and two sections of land. So the economic unit varies in different places, and one of the reasons why the last settlement scheme failed was that we sent the settlers into districts which were unsuitable for the kind of settlement these soldiers could undertake.
As regards the small holdings near the cities, we should be careful not to think of this as a solution. A certain number of people could be employed in that way near some cities. But when I was at Victoria, spending just one day there, I admit, in December of last year, I took the opportunity of visiting some of the soldier settlement farms and the farms which they had abandoned and which are now settled by British settlers on the Saanich peninsula, very near to Victoria. I found that the stories told there of these small holdings, where the settlers are supposed to work on the land during part of the year and then get supplementary 
employment in the city, were not dissimilar from the stories we hear from the soldier settlers on the prairies. We have had periods of unemployment in the cities, and during those periods there was no supplementary work to be had. In addition, the small holders found that the people in the city could not buy their fruits and vegetables when they were produced. Unless we can devise ways and means of planning our agricultural and our economic life so that our agriculture and industry may be supplementary to one another, and that one may absorb the products of the other, we shall not be able to make a scheme of this sort work satisfactorily.
One hon. member said a few moments ago that Great Britain was bringing a great deal of land under the plough and that she would assist in the feeding of Europe. I do not think that is quite what the bulletin or the government had in mind. I suggest this, that Great Britain will be much more self-supporting after this war than she has ever been before. One who has been there can readily see that land which was never ploughed before, or not ploughed for many years, is now under the plough. In the county of Devonshire from which I come, when I went back there for a day I drove over land which I remembered as park land, land over which deer ran, and I saw this land now ploughed up. I know that when this war ends, the agricultural production of this country will be quite sufficient, and we must not make the mistake of settling men upon the land after the war unless they are thoroughly suitable for that kind of work and unless we can provide them with transportation facilities or find markets for what they produce.
I am hoping that when the war does end, the nations of the world will get together and formulate plans for international trade and commerce which will stabilize that commerce, and stabilize agricultural production to a degree. While I think we are wise to consider plans of this kind during the war, because if peace comes suddenly and we have no plans made for any of our returned men, we are going to be in a very bad position, I want to emphasize, in discussing this particular measure, that we must not consider a scheme of this kind to be any solution even for the 16 per cent of the men who have signified their desire to go back to the land after the war. Much more must be done, and that much more involves the larger picture of the economic structure of this country. I do not like to see this question being discussed apart from the larger picture. We must make sure that plans of this kind fit into the whole picture of Canadian economy

Veterans' Land Act
when this war ends. There is no question that we are then going to be faced with conditions such as we have never faced before. The old methods of laissez-faire have undoubtedly gone for good; whether we like it or whether we dislike it, we are going to be faced with economic planning in practically every country of the world, and we ourselves will have to fit into that picture somehow. I warn the minister and the committee that, while it is wise to discuss plans of this description, we should not look upon them as being in the nature of a solution of the great problem which will face us at the end of this war.
I too, like the hon. member for Battle River, do not propose to go to-day into the whole soldier settlement scheme. I want to say something about it when the appropriate minister is before the house with his estimates, and although he is in his seat now, I do not propose to get that far out of order. The experience of the soldier settlers under the earlier scheme will interfere with the promotion of a scheme of this description. I believe that in the districts where soldier settlers inhabit such places as I have mentioned this afternoon, the very fact of the miserable conditions under which these people live did interfere at the beginning with our recruiting. I have heard young men say, "Look what happened to the men who gave up everything in the last war; see where they are now." In some instances these boys came from places just like that. I know that owing to the progress of the war and the intensification of recruiting efforts, as well as to some extent the economic pressure which was discussed here last night, many of these boys have joined up. But when they come back, though they themselves were bom in rural localities, they are not going to risk getting into the condition in which their parents were or in which people on the land have been right up to the present time.
What I have said applies not only to the soldier settlers but to the agricultural industry very generally. The farmer, it is said, throughout history has always been the forgotten man. He was the slave, the peon, the hewer of wood and the drawer of water. I do not believe that our society can exist and go forward industrially unless we lay the foundations of prosperity in the rural and agricultural areas of our country. That involves much more than a scheme for putting people back on the land; it involves a reorganization of our economic system in such a manner that the farmer will be guaranteed a reasonable return for the labour which he expends and for the knowledge which he puts into his land and into his effort.
While I am going to support this measure now in committee, I want to have it clearly understood that, as far as we are concerned, we want a scheme which will fit into a larger economic scheme to deal with the rehabilitation of the country when the war ends.

I deprecate their manner of speaking, not only for that reason, but also because of the state of mind which it may bring about among our young men who are now in the forces and those who will enlist later. Time after time I have sat here and heard hon. members trying to make out a case for condemning a whole region and a whole government administration, on the strength of one incident arising in some settlement out west or elsewhere in this country.
The leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation has just pointed to conditions in some shacks. When the hon. gentleman was still in Britain and in swaddling clothes, I, for one, lived in a shack of that kind, homesteading with my father, some fifty years ago. But in those days we did not have
Veterans' Land Act

the hon. gentleman's kind of party to offer us something for nothing. We did not have the sort of policy which seeks to have the government do something for you. We had spirit and courage of the kind which developed the great west, qualities which are still available to make a success of a measure such as the government proposes to introduce.
I wish to support the hon. member for Peace River, whose constituency adjoins mine. I desire also to say something to the committee, the minister and the government about the district which I represent. I beg the indulgence of hon. members if in the short time at my disposal I refer frequently to that particular part of the country, because it contains a great deal of land; and no matter what the hon. member for Melfort may say, or how successful a farmer he may be, I contend that if you put the right man on the right land, such as we have in our district, he can make a living, and a fairly good one.
Hundreds of friends of mine throughout that north land are making a decent living on quarter-sections and half-sections. I say to the hon. gentleman that if he is looking for a fortune, if he wants to make a lot of money, it is useless for him to go on any kind of land, be it homestead or any other kind. Let him join the Canadian Pacific Railway Company or something of that sort. What are we offering our young men to-day, these men who are braving difficulty and danger? Are we going to tell them that they are afraid to go on a piece of land? After offering their lives in the greatest and noblest cause for which any man can venture his life, are they to be told that they have not the courage of their ancestors to go to the lands in the west which are still available and make homes for themselves as their fathers did before them?

speechtext:
I have before me the
figures of the last census. Although probably some hon. members who have spoken to-day come from districts which people are leaving, I may say that the constituency of Athabaska showed the largest increase in population in the last ten years of any part of Canada, bar none, not even excepting the far-famed Peace River. We showed practically one-quarter of the entire increase of population in Alberta, and we would have shown a larger increase than that had not the provincial government, with the usual sanity shown by

that government, cancelled some years ago the homestead policy so that to-day there is no more homestead land to be secured in that province.
Those who have condemned the proposed scheme but who say they will vote for it have forgotten that the government are doing what should have been done after the last war. What I am saying now is not a condemnation of the government of that day. The minister in charge of the bill said last night that it was a new venture, that no organization had previously been set up such as we are preparing to erect now in order to provide men going on the land with proper information as to location, the nature of the soil, the possibilities of the district, transportation and so forth. The government to-day are preparing to do all that. We are telling our boys that there will be made available for them an organization fully informed and capable of directing them in any province where land is still available.
From a point 25 miles northeast of the town in which I live the railway plan, as mentioned by the hon. member for Peace River, showed possibilities and indicated what the directors of the two great railway companies thought of that north country from the point of view of future settlement and development. The Canadian Pacific railway for a great many years had no interest in the northern part of Saskatchewan and Alberta until about 1925, and during that time the northern half of those provinces were considered Canadian National territory. Branches were built by the Canadian National Railways from Prince Albert and Edmonton, north, east and west. Later on, in 1927, 1928 and 1929, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company secured charters for lines from Prince Albert in a westerly direction, and a line was constructed to a point 25 miles west of Meadow Lake. The Canadian National Railways constructed north-easterly from Edmonton in the direction of the town in which I live, and the railway is in operation. They had a charter to build a line to St. Walburg, Saskatchewan, and another branch from my home town to join the Canadian Pacific railway at a place known as Beaver Crossing on the Beaver river. They obtained running rights to a place near Loon Lake, and from a point north of Beaver river the Canadian Pacific railway continued in a north-westerly direction to Lac La Biche, to join with the Northern Alberta Railways, leading eventually to a western outlet. It was a vast plan. Surveys were made; plans were all prepared, and when the crash came in 1929, both companies were preparing to give contracts to build

Veterans' Land Act
these different lines. I have available for the committee figures with regard to homestead land at that time which was still capable of settlement in that country. These lands constitute a large area and are productive. The rainfall is almost certain every year, and there is a fair amount of merchantable timber so that the homesteader can earn a few dollars in the winter time. There are a large number of lakes filled with commercial fish-white -dish, trout and so on-and the farmers can work thereat in the fall and the winter and earn some money. With the hon. member for Peace River I realize that the time is not propitious to ask the government to build railways, but the construction of necessary lines should form a part of the enterprise, because plans exist already. They relate to a part of the country which was known to be productive; it was known to have possibilities of earning sufficient to meet any expenditures that might be made in developing it and to justify a railway line extending all the way from Prince Albert into the Peace River and Cariboo country.
The failures of the last settlement scheme have been admitted by everybody. Unfortunately, as a result of lack of preparation, mistakes were made at that time for which we cannot blame the board to-day, nor could wc have blamed them for many years past. I have had many negotiations with the soldier settlement board and have found them willing at all times to meet the settler more than half way. Any man who was willing to do his best found sympathetic treatment on the part of the board, wherever he might happen to be. The trouble was, however, that the purchases were made at a time of inflation. I realize that, unfortunately, human nature is the same everywhere, and I am afraid it will be the same after this war. A good many men who had some influence locally or with the then government took charge of the organization and the placing of settlers. In the district where I live, I can say that at least 150 men were placed all the way from Smoky Lake to Cold Lake. Some of the land was purchased through the agency of some men who had influence with the then government. The result was that land that was not suitable was purchased, and chattels were bought at prices that were far too high while stock was sold at ridiculous figures. I remember a team of horses that sold for between five and six hundred dollars and an ordinary cow sold for $150. That is sufficient to show that there was no possibility of any success. But where the soldier himself used his head, or where he was fortunate enough to fall into the hands of some man who wanted to be fair, he was
able to succeed. I can point out in that district dozens of men who have made good on the land and who to-day are happy. They own their land, or at any rate they owe very little on it. They make first-class citizens, and they are the type of men who are most needed in the west. The returned men who went into that part of the country, after serving overseas and risking their lives, exerted a very beneficial influence among the foreign population of western Canada. They are the type of people I love and admire, for they helped to develop the western plains. Those people from other lands who do not speak our own language and had not the same customs came into contact with our returned men and were helped to a wonderful degree. Our soldier settlers inculcated in them a love of the flag and of our institutions. They have done a great deal to build up the national edifice which we have been trying to rear in northern Alberta and Saskatchewan.
I am the father of a family; I have many close relatives in the forces, and some of them might possibly take advantage of this scheme. I want to congratulate this government upon the method they are adopting under this resolution of bringing back into trade and industry the boys who went out from here and making provision that those who are fit to go on the land can take advantage of the lands available in Canada, as well as upon the other bill providing for vocational training, which together will provide that every one of our boys upon his return will have some place to go and make a decent living after the war.
But is it right for some hon. members to paint such a terrible picture of what is going to happen to us after the war? Is it a proper thing to try to discourage these men, whether in Canada or overseas, to say that the country will not be able to take care of them when the war is over, to induce them to believe that we no longer have the Canadian spirit, that we have lost the courage and initiative of our ancestors, who from the waters of the Atlantic to the sunny slopes of the Pacific and from the gulf of Mexico to the Arctic created civilization and progress on this continent? I believe there will be a new deal after the war. The government is now preparing to bring about this new deal. No matter what my hon. friends directly opposite me say, I believe that to take one example out of thousands of something they evidently do not like and base criticisms of the government upon that is not fair. We want to offer the young men of this country something better than that.

Veterans' Land Act

Since I am rambling on about myself, may I say that my ancestors have belonged to this country since 1632. When the foundations of the city of Montreal were laid, my ancestors were already established on the soil of Canada. I have never despaired of Canada. Even in the darkest days of the depression in 1930-32 when I was a member of the local house in Alberta I moved a resolution as an appeal to the people and particularly to the youth of Canada. It was very discouraging in those days, there seemed to be nothing for the people to do; at one time they were told to tighten their belts and at another time they were told they were too choosy. But I believe we shall never see those things again. We are now offering these chances of resettlement and building homes on the land. I should like to try with these young men to lift a corner of the veil which hides the future of the country I have the honour to represent. It is absurd to say that there are no possibilities here. There are great opportunities for those who come back; with this whole world to be reconstructed and fed, there will be tremendous opportunities for the young men and the young women. I am convinced that there will be more opportunities after this war for those with ambition and courage than we have had in this country for many decades. I say to the young men who are in the forces and to those who, unfortunately, perhaps because of physical defects are unable to join, do not listen to the proposition that this world will not be fit to live in after the war. I resent and deprecate and reject the libels being expressed on the floor of this house against Canada, its possibilities and its people.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say just a few words in support of the measure before the committee, one which I believe to be a sincere attempt to deal with the very difficult problem of rehabilitation. The minister in his most lucid statement of yesterday explained to the house that for months a committee had been sitting considering the various phases of this matter, and as a consequence of their work he is now presenting to the house what is believed to be the best way with which the matter can be dealt.
I do not think the fact that the Soldier Settlement Act following the last war was to a considerable extent a disappointment, if not indeed a failure, is any reason why we should not try again. We shall benefit from the mistakes made at that time, and avoid the pitfalls which exposed our soldiers to disappointment in their effort to rehabilitate themselves-.
There are one or two features in connection with this matter with which I should like to deal particularly. I was glad this afternoon to hear the minister say that the bill would be wide enough to include men who wished to have a small lot of an acre or two which, I presume, could be extended to ten acres. These would be lots where they could live and enjoy rural life, and at the same time assist in maintaining their families while, for a portion of the year, they might be occupied in some industry in a neighbouring town. I hope that this will be considered also from the point of view of the rural districts. I have in mind the necessity of having community centres such as one used to see in France. During the last war I had an opportunity of visiting various parts of rural France. I had also seen them on previous occasions, and each time I had

Veterans' Land Act
been impressed with the methods employed by the French people in the rural districts to obtain, the maximum agricultural production, and at the same time to maintain community life. The people who are conducting the farms do not live on their farms, but maintain themselves in little settlements or communities where they can enjoy the privileges of social life, and bring up their children under those conditions, with schools and churches conveniently located, and with the advantages offered by stores and other opportunities which would be denied them if they were living in remote districts of the country.
Another thing in this connection which has appealed to me as a farmer, is that there should be more cooperation among neighbouring farmers. Surely it should be possible in a community of that kind to have many of the agricultural implements used in common, and arrangements made whereby at harvesting time reapers could be used in common to cut the grain quickly on the various farms. Then, later on, there would be the cooperative method of threshing and marketing the grain. It seems to me a great deal of labour is wasted through lack of cooperation. Although I do not always see eye to eye with the cooperative movement to my left, I believe there is much to be learned and much advantage to be derived from a cooperative movement in many phases of agriculture.
An example of this type of cooperation is found in the Antigonish movement in Nova Scotia. This is under the direction of St. Francis Xavier university and was started in the summer of 1927 by twelve farmers who got together to discuss what they could do to improve their crops and income for the next year. By meeting together during the -winter and discussing their problems and cooperating one with the other, they were able in the following year to sell the product of their farms for $5,300, a sum which had not been possible to realize previously. That work was continued, and it has extended until the present time. I was very much interested in the movement there, because it included housing as well. It was found that by a cooperative effort they were able to build their houses at a much reduced cost, and thereby provide much needed housing which they were not able to obtain in any other way.
I was sorry to learn that the Dominion Housing Act had ceased to function, and I suggest that under this measure it will be necessary to provide housing as well as land. If these smaller allotments are given to
returned men, some provision will have to be made to house them, and it should be quite easy to work out a housing plan in connection with the -measure the minister is now introducing by way of resolution.
I should like to express my entire agreement with the sentiment expressed this afternoon by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar when he said that this should be part of a general scheme to improve the lot of the farmer. Farmers throughout the country have had a difficult time to make a living, and we all know quite well that many of them have struggled for a lifetime only to find at the end of their days that they still have large mortgages on their farms.
During the last year in the county of Durham some sixty farmers had to abandon their farms. Most of those were 100-acre farms, which means a loss in productive capacity of some 6,000 acres. It was not a question of selling their farms, but rather one of abandoning them altogether. Therefore, when the government is looking for farms it will find a few in the county of Durham already available at a very small price. Perhaps they could be acquired by the payment of taxes.
My leader expressed my views very clearly to-day-extraordinarily well, in fact, considering that he knows nothing about farming; all of which goes to show that a lawyer can always have a brief.

My few remarks on this resolution are prompted by some discussion that took place early in the afternoon regarding assistance to be given to men who are interested only in small holdings of perhaps one, two or five acres. I should like to refer briefly to that aspect of the proposal. If I understood the minister's reply correctly, it appears that it will be necessary for these holdings to be located within reach of industry where the settlers may be able to secure employment. I should like to suggest that consideration be given to placing men in small homes wherever they may want to settle.
After all, I suppose it is the ambition of nearly every man to own his home during his lifetime, but only a small percentage are able to achieve that ambition. There is a growing population of small home owners, men who have perhaps only one acre of land out in the country, sometimes four or five miles from even a village. I have been interested in noting how these people, with only a very small amount of cash, seem to be able to get along, raise a family and in some cases educate their daughters to be schoolteachers. If a man owns a home out in the country, his taxes may not amount to more than $5 a year. He has no rent to pay. If he has a

Veterans' Land Act
good cow, he gets his milk and butter and has skim-milk to feed to his hogs and hens. He will have butter to sell, because it would not need an awfully good cow to produce sufficient milk for that. Then he will have his eggs. If he keeps four hogs and sells two, the return from the two will pay the cost of feeding the four. If he knows how to butcher and smoke his meat, he will have meat that really costs him nothing. If he is industrious, he will be able to get what fuel he requires without having to pay out any cash. He will not have to buy any vegetables because he could grow his potatoes and other vegetables on his land. The result is that at the end of the year he finds that he does not need very much cash to make a living.
I have an interesting example I should like to give the committee to show just how little cash it takes to keep a man and his wife and family. This particular man happened to be working for me, and I asked him how much cash it took to keep him and his family for a year. He had not any idea. I asked him about his taxes, and he told me that because he lived in the village, they were $23.50. I asked, him about his cow, and he said that he had had to buy one bag of chop which cost him $1.70. I asked him about his hay, and he told me that he had cut it along the roadside and had been able to get plenty. He told me that he never had to pay cash for wood and that he was able to grow enough vegetables. After we had gone on for some time I said, "If you had $100 cash, would that be all you would require for one year?" He said, "Oh, yes; that would be plenty." Then I went in to see his wife. This was near Christmas. I asked her about the matter. When I mentioned the $100, she almost screamed. "Lornie has not given me one cent since the cow freshened last spring," she said, "and I have kept the house and myself and Phyllis on what we made from that cow." I told that to a member of parliament, the then member for Southeast Grey, I think it was, and she was horrified that people should live under such conditions. I said, "Tell me what is wrong. They have a nice, clean house and always have plenty of good food. They have meat and vegetables and fruit-everything that any person would want. Their clothes are always nice and clean. They have a good stove, a nice couch, and good beds to sleep in. What more can you ask?" Sometimes they have a radio and they own a car.
I give this, Mr. Chairman, just as an example of the small amount of cash that a person needs to live on if he has a little home of his own and can grow some of his own food, and so I would say to the minister and to hon. members, do not be too anxious to see that the returned men shall settle on land near an industrial centre. If, instead, they keep away from the city and go out into the country, no matter how far out they may go, they can always find work because some farmer in the community is always wanting an extra hand, and in addition there is road work and the lumber camps, so that they never need be out of work. It is not every man who is capable of taking one or two hundred acres of land and making a success of farming. There are men who can get along very nicely in some trade who could not make a success of a farm if you gave it to them, fully equipped, and so I would suggest that consideration be given to these small holdings. They do not cost much.
I had a man working for me last summer and he was preparing to build a good home. He had been paying rent, and he had built a little building in which to store his furniture while he was working for me. I suggested to him in the fall that he warm up that place and live in it for the winter. He was a handy man; he did that, and he told me afterwards that his wife was never so happy as she had been in that little house. He said, "You would hardly notice the small amount of fuel it took to keep the place warm." I said, "Is the place big enough?" and he replied, "Sure, there is lots of room." I suppose that little home did not cost him much more than $35 cash because he had his own lumber. They had two children, and they were comfortable and happy there. So we should not get into our minds that we need to be extravagant in our ideas of settlement. Let us help a man to find some sort of home that he can call his own so that he will be freed from the anxiety of always wondering whether he is going to be able to find the rent at the end of the month. We do not need to be too anxious to settle him near some industrial town or big city. I think very often we would be well advised to keep him as far away from the city as possible.

I had not intended to say anything on this resolution, Mr. Chairman, but I am concerned over some of the suggestions that have been made to the minister in regard to the various schemes that might be included under this measure. I want to be as helpful as possible to the minister because I know he is anxious to make a good job of rehabilitation. And rightly so, because it is one of the most important jobs that could be given any minister. We have to have a proper organization of life after the war for the men who are demobilized from our armed forces and for those now engaged in war production-it is either that or chaos. I -think the minister should be commended for making a beginning on this problem now. But I am afraid that we cannot mix a small holdings scheme with a land settlement scheme where a man is supposed to pay for the land and become self-supporting after a certain period. On a small -holding a man cannot produce enough to make his own living, let alone pay for the land. It seems to me they are two separate things altogether. The one scheme will be on a sort of charitable basis, it seems to me, and the other is to a large extent a commercial venture. I would suggest to the minister that he should not promise too much in order to be accommodating. These matters should be looked into very carefully to guard against spoiling one scheme by widening it to include the other. I am not suggesting that nothing should be done in the way of small *holdings, but I do suggest that it should be kept separate from the real land settlement scheme.
We should remember also that any land settlement scheme to-day must be undertaken in the light of a full knowledge of the social and economic conditions prevailing. Many people when they talk about land settlement refer to what our fathers and grandfathers did in settling the land, and they overlook entirely the fact that conditions are quite dissimilar to-day. I was brought up on a pioneer farm where we saw very little money but where we could live fairly well because what we consumed was produced on the farm. We produced our own wheat, took it to the grist mill and had it ground into flour, and the flour -was baked at home. We produced our own potatoes and vegetables, raised our own mutton, pork and beef. Of course we also had quite a bit of herring which we had to buy, except that in the spring of the year we caught a few. I have seen my mother shear the sheep, card the wool and knit it. She could not weave, but a neighbour woman would do the weaving.

All that is changed to-day. We have such and such a company to do our laundering, another company to do our baking, and all the time we are being pressed to have somebody else do our darning, mending and all that. The old life is changed. The farmer to-day requires money to pay for everything which was formerly produced in the household. That money has to come from somewhere. It must be produced on the farms through the sale of agricultural products, or come as income from some other source. If we are to have a land setlement scheme under which those who go on the land are supposed after a year or two to be self-supporting, they will have to be provided with fairly large tracts, depending upon the particular kind of farm product they intend to produce, and there will have to be a market for what they produce.	.
I advise the committee not to be too sanguine of the success of any venture of this kind. The fact that we are living in a machine age is as true of agriculture as of any other kind of production. The more agricultural machines you have, the fewer farmers you will require. So, when the scheme is all ready, the continued improvement in farm machinery will result in a greater volume of farm products than can be sold, and our problem will not have been solved; it will have just begun. I make this first suggestion to the minister with the best of intentions, and recognizing that the minister wants to help the person with a small income who hopes to add to his living by having a small holding, but I do not think we should include the two kinds of settlement under the same bill.
Another thing he should remember is that the farmers of Canada by and large are in a bad way. I believe I am right in saying that one-half of the farmers of British Columbia are not self-supporting on the land and must have some kind of other work in order to keep going. There are those here from British Columbia who may know a little more about farming in that province than I do, but I have travelled through the province, and I am quite convinced that not more than half the farmers support themselves wholly f-rom their farms.

The farmers of
British Columbia have been mentioned so I should like to say a word, although I had not intended to say anything until we got into committee on the bill. I heard an Ontario farmer talking about putting a man in a S35 shack. I wonder how many recruits we shall get for our magriificent air force if they think that all we are going to offer them when they return is a $35 shack to live in. I wonder how many recruits we are going to get to join other branches of the service if we tell them that we propose to send them up to the Peace River district, no matter how far it may be, perhaps away in the wilderness. The proposition is not reasonable. I have not heard many returned soldiers speak in this connection. I am not going to talk at this time about the soldier settlement board, for I do not think this is the proper occasion, when we are discussing the present resolution. I may have something to say about the board later.
It seems to me that we are wasting a lot of time. Perhaps I am wasting some now. We have to win this war before we settle anybody. If any hon. member supposes that after this war these young men are going to be satisfied to be settled away off in some area forty miles from the nearest contact with civilization, he is badly mistaken. Speaking as a farmer member, I say that the hon. member for Vancouver East is correct in his reference to the position of farmers in British Columbia, except that I would say that 75 per cent, rather than 50 per cent, have not been able to support themselves solely from their farms. There is hardly an area to which that statement does not apply, with the possible exception of the Okanagan. I doubt if it does not apply there as well; But in the rest of British Columbia 80 per cent of the farmers have heavy mortgages and are behind in their taxes. Before you can settle these men on the land, the first thing you have to do is to find a market at proper prices for what the farmers produce. Apparently, from what was said by my good friend the hon. member for Renfrew North, or one of these millionaire districts in Ontario, all the farmers there are prosperous. But I should like to mention one farmer who came from that district to my district last year. He is one of these city farmers, with a big fortune behind him. We have 'been told by one hon. member from Ontario that eggs can be produced at a profit at nine cents a dozen. I may refer to a letter written by this city farmer who had a big business behind him, with regard to the fortune which could be made in the Fraser valley. This man found that things turned out very differently; he had
to sell all his cows and all his other live stock, and he is now subdividing his property and selling it in five-acre plots. It is very easy for people in other lines of business to talk about the fortunes to be made in farming.
I am going to support any bill which will help to rehabilitate returned men, but the minister or anyone else who knows anything about returned men knows in the first place that you are not going to be able to talk to the young soldier coming back from this war as you talked to the soldier of the last war. It is all very well to say, "Here is this magnificent pioneer area for you to develop. Your grandfather did that sort of thing and now you do it." Possibly he should pioneer, but do you think he will be willing to do that? I say to my hon. friend who suggests building these mansions for $35 that I do not know where a man can make a living in British Columbia by working a small place and picking up jobs on the side. speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
The minister made a statement at another stage of this legislation. I do not think I was in the house at the time the statement was made. It was on the last day before the recess. I read' that statement with care, and I think I understood some of the underlying principles of this legislation. At the same time I am bound to say that a study of the bill and of the minister's statement confirms the impression which I formed when the matter was in the resolution stage that this is a very technical matter. Since I am not an expert in insurance law, I confess at once that I am not in a position to offer

War Risk Insurance

much if any contribution to this debate. Yet there are certain points which I think I should briefly point out.
The preamble asserts:
Whereas by reason of the state of war now existing there is risk of damage to property in Canada by enemy action.
That, of course, is a truism and, being true, it is expedient to bring in some measure such as that now before the house. I assume there has been some substantial public demand for this measure.
What apparently is contemplated is a limited measure of insurance for a limited sum covering a limited area of risk, and I assume that is as far as the government or the minister intends to go at the moment. I have not had time or opportunity to examine similar legislation in the United Kingdom, but I understand that over there the principles are very much more extended, because of the situation now and for some time past existing. That is natural and reasonable. Unquestionably the risk of damage to property from enemy action over there has been and is at the moment far in excess of anything contemplated here. If my understanding of the position is correct, based on announcements that have been made and the information I have received from members of the ministry, the anticipated damage to property here from jnemy action is limited to that arising from sporadic raids on our coast and not from invasion. That may not be a correct statement of the position taken by the military experts of the government, but so far as I have been able to learn the government policy in that regard, from the public utterances that have been made-I am not going to refer to private utterances that I have heard-that is as far as the staff officers of the Department of National Defence have gone in their preparations for our coastal defence. I am not raising any particular quarrel with that. How far short of reality that may be no one knows, least of all myself; the whole thing is in the lap of the gods, and much will depend on what happens in the next few weeks.
In any event I assume that the present bill is in response to a public demand, although I am bound to say that very little inquiry has been made of me, neither have I had any communication with anyone. But in the statement which the minister made he adverted to the inquiry that the ministry had made with respect to this matter, and I shall speak of that in a moment.
Dealing with the bill itself, and without attempting to go into the clauses, it will be noted that the bill enables the government itself to enter into contracts for war risk

insurance; that the terms of the bill are enabling. There is no compulsory provision. As a first venture in this new field it is perhaps as well that it should be merely enabling and not compulsory, because the whole thing, at least for a time, is in the experimental stage. Time and events will determine the wisdom of the venture and whether or not the scheme should be extended.
Section 3 of the bill sets up this enabling provision:
The minister may, on behalf of His Majesty, enter into a contract of insurance with any person to insure against the risk of war damage, any property in which such person has an insurable interest.
That, if I interpret it correctly, visualizes a department of government entering into the business of war risk insurance contracts.
But I do not understand that that is the primary object of the bill. If I appreciate the situation aright, the minister proposes to use section 4 or some other enabling power in the bill whereby the actual insuring will be done by insurance or casualty companies. I am assuming-and he will correct me if I am wrong, because I have not had him give me a technical explanation of the bill-that he intends to operate under section 4, whereby the minister is enabled to establish one or more schemes of insurance, as he sees fit; or that he may refer to a separate condition that may obtain against which insurance will be taken out along the lines of the war risk insurance visualized by section 3. I should like the minister to make that clear.
However, if any other concrete scheme of war risk insurance is contemplated being set up under the bill, that is to say if the minister has in mind any scheme of war risk insurance other than that contemplated by the provisions of section 3, read in conjunction with the other appropriate sections of the bill, then I think he should tell the house what he has in mind. If there be such other scheme in contemplation, then I suggest to the minister that in conformity with sound legislative practice and sound policy the principle of suoh other scheme should be set out in the bill itself, and should not be left to the minister or supervisor really to legislate other war risk insurance schemes never contemplated by parliament.
I may be entirely on the wrong tack in this matter. I am speculating to a degree, and I should like to have a little more precise information. If there be such other scheme in contemplation, then I suggest to the minister that the principles of such other scheme of insurance should be incorporated subsequently in the body of the bill, and that he should make that clear; because, according to my way

War Risk Insurance
of thinking, under the provisions of section 4, read in conjunction with section 32, the minister may set up a scheme entirely different from that contemplated by section 3. Or he may set up any number of schemes. I suggest with great respect-and I do not intend to be controversial or destructive, but rather to be constructive-that parliament ought not to give to any department of government blanket powers of this kind, even in wartime. Of course it is a fact that in wartime, necessities on occasions may require full plenary powers in certain spheres and capacities directly connected with the war. But this would not appear to be one of those occasions. If the minister has in mind the setting up of any other type of insurance, then I think it should be set out in the bill. That is the principal objection I desire to register at this moment to the bill itself.
As I said before, I do not wish to hedge about this thing, but I must say that the minister's intentions are not quite clear to me. In fact I think it is clear from his previous declaration that it was not the intention of the government to enter into actual contractual relations under the provisions of section '3, but to utilize the facilities of existing insurance companies.
I may be wrong as to that, but I believe that is a fair interpretation to be derived from his words. But if it be true, may I say that I am not condemning his suggestion. I think it is worthy of the most careful examination, because I am one who believes that private enterprise will do a better job than any government department in a purely business matter such as this. I think it will be handled better, and greater care will be taken. They have a stake in the matter, and they will exercise greater care in the whole contractual operation, right down to the point of settling. Private enterprise may not be able to take all the burden in this matter. I do not know how great the burden may be, measured in terms of dollars and cents, and it might be able to take on the financial obligations only at r prohibitive cost.
This is an experiment. When the proposal was before the house on March 27, the minister made a statement in which he indicated that the bill was presented after an exhaustive study of the problem from coast to coast, and that a report had been prepared for him by an eminent member of the legal profession whose name he did not mention. The report had been prepared after that gentleman had visited the Pacific coast, the maritime provinces, Quebec, Montreal and Washington. I
regret that the minister did not give the house the name of that eminent member of the legal profession.

He further stated that there had been full consultation with the official representatives of the fire and casualty insurance companies of Canada, and that with the aid of such advice and material the plan of war risk insurance and compensation as embodied in the bill had been formulated.
I commend the minister for the pains which I know must have been taken before this bill was drafted. At the same time I regret we were not given a copy of the report for our information before the legislation reached this stage. All of the minister's statements certainly indicate to me that there has been careful preparation of this bill-and that is as it should be.
The minister then went on to describe the British precedents, which no doubt are very helpful, although conditions there are vastly different from what they are here, and from what we hope they may continue to be. He also indicated the situation in the United States where a corporation has been set up under the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, and authority has been granted to pay over a sum not in excess of a billion dollars to the War Damage Corporation funds. He also indicated that New Zealand had

recently adopted compulsory war risk insurance based upon fire insurance policies already in force, as I gathered from his statement.
From what he said I gathered that what is indicated in Canada is a scheme based on the experience of some of these other nations, but very limited in its scope and application. The minister then laid down four principles which he stated were the basis of the bill: First, that the burden should be distributed equally across the country, because the whole nation is at war. Prima facie I should say that requires some further explanation. I am not dissenting from it; I can see sound reasons why it should be that way. It is a war risk that is being assumed, and the cost of that may be substantial, although perhaps not much in a given case. Being a war risk, it may be just to say that the burden of carrying that risk should be borne by the nation as a whole.
Then he went on to say that the second basic principle was that the insurance should be voluntary rather than compulsory. As a beginning, I do not think there can be much criticism of that principle. It is an experiment. I do not think we would want to put into effect a compulsory war risk insurance scheme. Without being able to measure in any degree the risk involved, a compulsory system is not justified in Canada at the moment.
The minister referred to the third principle which was that a certain .minimum coverage should be given to all home owners, householders and certain others without the payment of premiums. I am not just sure that that is sound. Per se I just cannot understand why those who have a certain minimum coverage or who come within certain classes of property owners should be free from the payment of any premiums. It may be that that is the system followed1 in other jurisdictions; I do not know, but at first blush I just cannot appreciate why there should be no premium cost to the owner. I cannot see that that is absolutely sound. After all, this is not to be a compulsory system, and it may be that there are sound reasons for that principle. I am not sure that it is absolutely sound having regard to the fact that under principle No. 2, the minister stated that no property owner is entitled' to compensation unless he along with other property owners has made a special contribution proportionate to the indemnity he would get. I just cannot seem to add up those two things.
The fourth principle enunciated by the minister was that the payment of indemnity

and compensation, except in cases of undue hardship or national importance, should be postponed until after the war. That is a pretty hard provision. I realize that the minister has stated that this is based on the theory that war needs must have priority, but there is an elasticity in the language with respect to the payment of indemnity and compensation except in cases of undue hardship or national importance. This will mean that certain persons will get paid and certain other persons will not be paid. That will give rise to great dissatisfaction. The phrase "cases of undue hardship" can be defined, but any significance can be given to the phrase "national importance." I just do not understand that particular class of case, and I think this should be made clear. Perhaps this is a matter that could very well be discussed in the banking and commerce committee. However, I do not expect to be able to attend the sessions of that committee, so I think I should make these observations here.
I do not think the time of payment should be left entirely to the discretion of any department of the government, or even to the minister. If there is a contractual obligation for which a premium has been paid, then I think there should be some stated time of payment. It should' not have to wait until a declaration is made. I suggest to the minister that the time of payment should be made certain in the bill or in the contract itself. Then the minister went on to say, as reported on page 1703 of Hansard of March 27:
The insurance policies will be issued by the existing fire and casualty insurance companies through their established agents.
That is what I was referring to before. If that is the settled policy of the government, I do not see why it is not incorporated in the measure itself. I have glanced over the measure, and I do not see anything to indicate that that is to be the line of policy adopted by the department in connection with this matter. As I said before, I offer this criticism, not in a spirit of opposition to the bill but because I believe that this is the proper method of legislating once a policy is laid down. The bill itself should, in concrete terms or in as concrete terms as possible, follow the theory and principle of the policy.
The bill provides for the deduction of premiums for income and excess profits tax purposes only to a limited extent. I should like to have from the minister on some appropriate occasion an explanation of why

War Risk Insurance
there is a limitation. The coverage will be small and the premiums cannot be great, relatively speaking, so I cannot see why there should be any limitation in the matter of deducting premiums for taxation purposes. I think that should be a legitimate expense. At least, that is the wTay it strikes me and I think it would so strike any business man. I do not blame the minister for trying to get all the revenue he can, but why penalize a man who takes the precaution of insuring his premises against war risk? Why not allow him to deduct the premiums just as he would deduct fire insurance premiums as a business expense? The minister has stated that he will recommend that the clause relating to the deductibility of premiums for income tax purposes should be discussed in the banking committee. He stated that he was not wedded to any particular view in regard to the matter and I gather, therefore, that he has an open mind on the subject.
My view is that in connection with business properties this should be deductible in full, taking into account the cost of operations. There may be some reason why there has to be a limitation, but it has not been made apparent to me. Section 28 provides:
The premium payable with respect to any contract of insurance shall, for the purposes of the Income War Tax Act and the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, be deductible as an expense of carrying on the business if the property insured under such contract of insurance is used in connection with and required for the purpose of the trade

I am not suggesting that there should be a deduction in connection with premiums paid on private homes. The section goes on:
-but such deduction shall only be allowed to the extent that the total taxes payable by the insured under the said act are thereby diminished by 40 per centum of the said premium.
I should like to have an explanation of why that limitation is there. Just what the effect of that overriding provision is, I do not know at the moment and I have not sought expert advice. I think we should have some further explanation from the minister.
There are other observations I should like to make with respect to other sections of the bill, especially section 32 which gives power to the governor in council to make regulations. This matter of legislating by regulation is becoming acute from time to time. I object to the principle, and I think the house ought to object to the principle of legislating by regulation or by order in council in connection with things that ought to be in the statutes themselves. I do not like the theory that a bureau of the government is to be
given from time to time the power of substantively enacting legislation, even within the ambit of the restrictions contained in the authorizing clause, unless it is absolutely necessary.
We are regulated to death to-day in matters in connection with the war. I believe that a large amount of that is necessary, but here you are giving power to an authority of government to put into these policies contractual obligations about which parliament knows nothing. They may be restrictions, or what not. Perhaps I am not expressing myself very well, but the principle, I say, is bad. I know it is the easiest thing in the world for government draughtsmen to put this class of clause in a bill. It is not new in this parliament; it is not new in the mother of parliaments. Hon. members who are students of legislation and of the law will recall a book that was written by a former Lord Chief Justice of England, Lord Hewart, under the title of "The New Despotism." I think I should register a protest on every occasion upon which I meet this form of despotism. I wish I could see some more evidence of being backed up by my colleagues in the legal profession. I am looking at one of them right now (Mr. St. Laurent), but I am not backed up at all.

I have no doubt my hon. friend has control of an ample supply of resources-if the government leaves him anything after he has paid his taxes.
I am not opposed to the principle of the bill, but I would hope that the banking and commerce committee will give it intensive study and that the proceedings of that committee will be public so that those of us who have not the opportunity of attending and participating in its proceedings may become familiar with what takes place and the recommendations advanced there from time to time. In this connection I would ask the minister to make available the report to which he referred and to which I have referred, also the recommendations made by the fire and casualty insurance companies who have been consulted, on the assumption that their recommendations have been made in writing.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want first of all to congratulate Mr. D'Arcy Leonard who was called in by the minister, and who has gone back through some 150 years of war risk insurance for the purpose of recommending a policy such as we have before us to-night. I also want to thank the insurance fraternity of Canada, all those managers, adjusters and other officers who have given freely of their time to Mr. Leonard in order that the government might be in a position to bring down this bill to be put before the banking and commerce committee for consideration. and I am sure that they will be willing to come forward and give their

services to the committee in order that we may get a workable measure. I personally take a little pride in having been able to expedite this measure because, being connected with the business myself, I have had a great many inquiries from time to time, and as hon. members know, I have frequently asked questions to ascertain how soon the government's policy might be brought down. While I compliment the minister upon bringing it down after making an announcement with respect to it on December 24, I think the delay has operated to a certain extent against our war effort. As I said in the house on a previous occasion, business men who have goods to send to the coast have always been a little fearful, having no insurance protection of this kind, that if anything happened to the goods they would be wiped out.
The minister stated to the house that the obligation to be assumed by the government under this legislation would be not more than $50,000 in any one case. Well, the people of this country may need the government to assume a greater obligation than $50,000, and I do not see the reason for fixing that sum when the bill says further on in section 27:
The minister shall refer to the advisory committee any application to enter into a contract of insurance under which the maximum amount of indemnity which may be payable exceeds two hundred and fifty thousand dollars.
I do not see why the minister says $50,000 in another place because, if we had passed this bill on December 24, we would be assuming obligations up to an amount of $250,000. I think the minister should make an announcement immediately to clarify that situation.
This question of war risk insurance is so vast and takes in so many subjects that it needs the greatest amount of discussion and the assistance of all the experts whom we can possibly get to formulate a bill and regulations which will be workable. After the banking and commerce committee have these regulations formulated, and after the advisory committee have done their work, the regulations should come back periodically to the house or to the banking and commerce committee so that the Canadian people will be informed of them and know where they stand. One of our greatest difficulties, as my leader said a little while ago, has been that so many regulations have been issued without the intervention of parliament. In connection with this business it is almost impossible to draft regulations which will be useful forever. For instance, you form a company of insurance and elect your board of directors; then you appoint

War Risk Insurance
your manager and your staff. Assume, for instance, that the House of Commons is the board of directors; the board cannot be telling the people who are running the business what regulations are going to be in force from time to time; certain rules of underwriting have to be followed. More especially in the present case, where we have something which is entirely new, and with no experience to guide us, we shall have to work by the method of hit-or-miss, and regulations will need to be formulated and revised from time to time.
In the bill it is provided that the minister shall appoint an advisory committee. My suggestion is that this be done, not by the minister, but by the insurance fraternity of Canada. They have done a pretty good job. Under the direction of the finest insurance department in the world, our Canadian insurance department directed by Mr. Finlayson, the insurance fraternity should pick out the people who are best suited for this job. The committee itself should designate the supervisor whom they think best fitted for this job. I believe that that course would remove a great many difficulties. There are thousands of agencies that wish to be consulted in this matter. The success of this scheme depends to a great extent on these agents. It is necessary that they shall be imbued with a patriotic spirit, so that they will be able to get people in Toronto, Saskatoon and Lake Centre, let us say, as well as those who are in hazardous areas such as Vancouver and Halifax, to take out insurance in view of the possibility of losing their property. There are only two ways of doing this. One is to give the agents a high enough commission; the other is to imbue them with a patriotic spirit so that the risk may be just tacked on to the fire insurance policies. By this means we could get a tremendous premium.
Who else are interested? Of course, we have the managers of all the companies in this country. There are the stock companies, the mutual companies, and the reciprocal companies. Each must be represented on the advisory board which we are going to set up. Besides them, we have the adjusters who must be consulted and induced to pick out their best men. If we do these things, we shall have success with this measure.
In reference to what the minister said about spreading the burden over the country, there are a great many ways of doing that. Take what New Zealand did. There, the burden is spread over all the people who have fire insurance policies. It just means that twenty-five cents per hundred dollars is added to each insurance policy. In Canada we have $12,000,000,000 of fire risks assumed by our companies.
If we had compulsory insurance, a ten cents per hundred rate would provide us with $12,000,000. It is not a very big rate; I do not know whether it is enough. A twenty-cent rate, of course, would give us $24,000,000. That is one way. We might have the voluntary method of getting premiums, and also we could follow the course of taking money from the consolidated revenue of the country. Where we take the money from the insured risk, most of that risk would bear on real estate. I hardly think it would be entirely fair, because the hazard is on both coasts and real estate would be bearing it; whereas by the other method each individual one of us would be benefiting by the hazard which the people on the coasts were taking. Therefore, perhaps a total voluntary system is not the best one. Under a wholly voluntary system we would have a specified premium which would be taken out only by those people who were under the hazard-we will say Vancouver and Saint John and Halifax. We should, therefore, require assistance from the consolidated revenue fund. Other things might be considered. Take wheat, which is shipped from west to east under warehouse receipt; compulsory fire insurance is necessary. We might have some compulsory, some voluntary, and some consolidated revenue fund.
We do not know how much money will be required; that is an unknown quantity. We do not know what the hazard is, and there is no experience to guide us. Our position is entirely different from that of Great Britain, Australia, or New Zealand. For these reasons I urge that the best insurance brains of this country be brought together in this committee, so that the necessary study may be made.
In passing, I might point out something which may be more important than property loss, and that is personal accident which may befall people on either or both coasts. I know, Mr. Speaker, that you and I would be quite willing to pay some premium in connection with any physical harm which might come to people who are on the coast and taking the brunt of the risk while we right here in the centre of the country are sitting pretty. That is another thing which must be thought about.
The thing is not as simple as we think. In Great Britain this whole business does not hinge simply on one form of insurance. It is not just a question whether you will insure your house or anything like that. In section 4 it is provided that the minister may establish one or more schemes of insurance as he sees fit. In Great Britain there are seven different schemes at the present time, and they need seven different kinds of people to take care of the risks involved. In this country
War Risk Insurance

we have not seven different schemes. We have not some of the things they have to insure, but we do need a wide range of experience.
With regard to legislation by order in council, I congratulate the minister upon having brought in a bill instead of proceeding to carry out the policy by order in council. I think that the more the light of day is thrown on the question, the better it will be for us; the more the House of Commons knows about it and the more discussion there is in the banking and commerce committee, the better.
There is a provision with regard to regulations. It will be perfectly impossible for us to sit down in the House of Commons-it is impossible for most of us at any rate-and formulate the underwriting principles which will be required in this vast field, which is a life study in itself. We shall, therefore, have to go to the banking and commerce committee, formulate the matter there as closely as we can with all the brains we have, and then leave it so that it may be subject to change.
As regards picking out the supervisor, there is a provision in section 2 that the minister may, with the approval of the governor in council, appoint an officer to be called the supervisor of war damage insurance and may, with such approval, fix the remuneration to be paid to him. I suggest that would be the greatest mistake. Let the advisory committee pick their own man. You might not even have to pay him; they might pay him themselves. I happen to know what wonderful cooperation has been given by the whole insurance fraternity. All the companies of Canada have offered to do the business for the country at cost and the agents will do the same. Let us utilize all their services.
One or two other questions which enter into the consideration of this subject might be interesting to the house. Take the question of compulsory insurance. Let us take a big oil company-we will not mention any names- a company that has a tremendous hazard, for instance, in Bedford basin. Is that company going to be allowed to insure its hazard there without insuring all the rest of its property all over Canada? This is one of the questions which must be considered by the insurance companies and by the banking and commerce committee. Take a mortgage company which has an interest in mortgages throughout the country from Vancouver to Halifax. Will they be allowed to insure only their risks in Vancouver and Halifax, or must they insure all over the country? These are some of the questions that have to be considered. I am saying this only to illustrate the vastness of the whole subject and to show how necessary it is for us to enlist the best brains.

I do not like legislation by order in council, but I think it would be a very great mistake to tie the hands of the committee to be appointed.
One last word. Insurance is a matter of trust and faith as between individuals and companies, and we must have that in this case. You cannot lay down rules and regulations that will be iron-bound. We must have it the other way. It is provided that the minister shall as soon as possible, but within three months after tihe termination of each year ending on the 31st day of March, submit an annual report to parliament covering the business affairs of the minister under this measure for the twelve months ending on the said 31st day of March. I suggest that the committee to be appointed should be responsible for expenditures. Leave it to them. Let them do the job under the control of the superintendent of insurance, and then you will have something that is worth while. I certainly commend the bill to the house.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
I
wish to support the hon. member who has just sat down (Mr. Ross, St. Paul's) on his suggestion that $50,000 is too small a sum to carry this policy. If Vancouver or Halifax were bombed for an hour, $50,000 would be a mere fleabite in satisfying the demands that would be made. Even if it were $200,000, the same thing might apply.
I want to accept the challenge of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), although I am not a member of the legal profession. He challenged support from any member of his own profession-he narrowed it down to that- in his opposition to legislating too much by way of regulation. As one who has suffered many things for many years from that practice, I heartily endorse him, lawyer or no lawyer. Someone once said, "Let me make the poems of a country and I care not who makes the laws." I would say, let me make the regulations under an act and I do not care who makes the act, because I have seen the whole spirit and sense and purport of an act crucified by regulation. It is something that lends itself to abuse. It is necessary to have some regulations, for there are very few acts which do not require something of the kind. Section 32 says that the governor in council may, on the recommendation of the minister, make regulations, and it gives three or four specific instances. One would think they were fairly limited to these things, but it goes on to say:
(a) as to the manner of making and the forms of policies. . . .
That seems as if it would confine it to the form of the policy, but under the Old Age Pension Act the same provision is put in,

War Risk Insurance
giving them power to draw up the application form. Of course the application form must or should be limited by the terms of the act. But what did they do? They said the act gave them power to make an application form and to put anything in that application form they chose. And they did, and nearly made a new act. I am glad to see that in the last few weeks the British Columbia supreme court granted an appeal brought forward on behalf of a poor old age pensioner and decided that these autocratic bureaucratic regulations must not override the actual meaning and intent of the act. While I admit that you must have some regulations, they ought to be limited as far as possible and their abuse prevented.
I understand that by regulations made some months ago or perhaps a year ago, provision was made that any damage to life or person of seamen or fishermen, or to their boats I think, should be compensated; I presume such personal injury does not come under this bill which deals wholly with insurance of property against damage and war risk. This is considered important enough to call for a special act. The other protection is even more important inasmuch as it relates to human life, the protection of fishermen and I think other people too who lose their life or are maimed by bombing or enemy action; would the minister not deem that sufficiently important to deal with by a separate act also? Because regulations might come and go, sometimes they go with the government or the individual who formulated them. It would be more satisfactory to have such an important matter concerning the lives of a great many fishermen on our coasts dealt with by statute also.
