speechtext:
Then I wish to refer to
cases where there has been damage done by aircraft of the Canadian air training plan. My understanding of the situation is that there is a committee which has power to make settlements, but there is no statute governing the matter, and therefore an individual whose
property or person might suffer damage is entirely dependent on what might be termed a charitable attitude of mind on the part of this committee. There have been cases where very substantial loss has occurred from falling aircraft, in some instances British aircraft, associated, I assume, with the commonwealth air training scheme. I can give two examples. I am speaking only from memory, but I believe that in the province of Quebec a farmer, or perhaps the better term would be a truck farmer or vegetable grower, had his barn destroyed by fire resulting from a British aircraft crashing. I think the British representatives in Canada have power to make settlements up to 81,000; but if the loss exceeds 81,000, then the whole circumstances must be reported to the authorities in the old country for decision. Naturally that takes many months, and very substantial loss does accrue to an individual in waiting for a settlement. In this man's case the insurance company made a token payment of $200, but that would not replace his barn or equipment or seed, and therefore he is left in an unfortunate position.
In another case, I believe in Ontario, a falling aircraft destroyed a boathouse, and two persons lost their lives. We have no statute fixing the responsibility in such cases. If I am correctly informed, in both the United States and Great Britain there is a statute covering such incidents. As we now have one of the most extensive air training schemes in the world, such cases are likely to increase, and I do not think it should be left to the discretion of any committee to deal with these important and difficult matters. We have some insurance companies that now include damage by falling aircraft in their coverage; but a large number of insurance companies are not prepared to accept that class of risk, very largely because they are dependent, as I have stated, upon a charitable attitude of mind on the part of the committee as to whether compensation can be secured for such loss.
Therefore, if it is not the intention of the minister to institute a scheme to cover such damage, then I believe a separate bill should be introduced to cover matters of this kind, because Canadian citizens are suffering great inconvenience and substantial loss in the time intervening before settlement is made. For example, if an aircraft destroys some fruit trees, the committee has power to make settlement. One of the bases of settlement is that the identity of the aircraft must be established. That is sometimes very hard to do. If a bus or truck or automobile has an accident, then the operator of the vehicle
War Risk Insurance

must remain at the scene of the accident. But it would not be possible for the pilot of an aircraft to remain at the scene of the accident, because there would not be landing facilities there. The law should provide that where an aircraft does damage, there is an onus upon the pilot to report as soon as he reaches his destination that he had an accident which resulted in damage to life or property. I am firmly convinced that it is time a statute be enacted in order fully to cover such a condition as I have outlined.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
In rising to take part in the discussion with respect to Bill No. 56, I may say I was much impressed by reading to some extent the discussions which took place upon a bill involving to a limited degree the legislation passed by the British House of Commons in 1941, known as the War Damage Act. As was pointed out to-night by the leader of the opposition, there are very substantial differences and distinctions as between the principles of this bill and the principles embodied in the legislation in the old land. For one thing, the question of compulsory insurance has not been adopted by this government in the legislation which is now before the house.
Like my leader, at this stage I am not in a position to suggest to the government that at the moment in Canada there should be anything like compulsory insurance of war risks. But the government might very well give consideration to the extension of the legislation, as time and circumstances may dictate, so that if it should become necessary in Canada for some compulsory form of insurance on war risks, it could readily be enacted, and we could be prepared for such a step.
I wish, however, to voice my opposition to the method by which this legislation is to be carried out. I do not know that I would have objected quite so vehemently against the principle of the carrying out of the legislation in this particular instance were it not for the fact that it followed in a long trail of regulations which are attached to our legislation from time to time. Surely it is becoming clearer from day to day to hon.
members that this chamber is dealing with______
well, I was going to say matters of almost minor importance, in some instances, in connection with our whole war effort administration.
When the War Measures Act was first brought into operation during this war the object most hon. members had in giving it their support was that it would be a 
convenience and an accommodation to the government. In addition to that, we felt it would be of tremendous advantage in the event of any emergency which might have developed from the war. But I do not believe private members generally ever expected the government of Canada to utilize the provisions of the War Measures Act to the extent to which they have been utilized in the last two and a half years. Furthermore, they have extended the principle embodied in the War Measures Act in bills such as this one, and have left nothing but a skeleton for us to deal with in the house, and they have relegated almost the entire legislation to regulations.
I protest against that, because it seems to me that we are not following the precedent established by parliament in the old country. I have before me the War Damage Act of 1941 passed by the parliament of the United Kingdom. This is an act which was debated for many days, and which consists of 102 sections. That was the bill passed in the United Kingdom, as opposed to this bill of only 34 sections now before us. It seems to me that even if we eliminate the matter of compulsory insurance which was embodied in the United Kingdom act, we have not left to this parliament the proper scope and proper sphere of legislative activity to which this chamber and parliament are justly entitled.
The minister may attempt to justify the regulations on the basis that this is more ot less an experiment in war risk insurance. Nevertheless the principle of government by order in council is there. Here again we have the principle of government by regulation instead of by the people. After all, we cannot treat lightly the trend taken by the government with respect to matters which I think might most appropriately form part of the discussion in this chamber.
In Great Britain the history of war risk insurance was one of slow movement. In the first instance there was a commission headed by Lord Weir which investigated the question of war risk insurance in the old land. In those earlier days that commission brought in a report opposing such a scheme, but that report was subsequently overruled, and the act to which I referred a few moments ago was the first step toward protecting the people in matters of that kind. The War Damage Act of Great Britain embodied not only the question of business principles but went almost to the root of the entire social fabric itself.
At this time I should like to read to the house one paragraph from the debates on that bill which took place in the British House

War Risk Insurance
of Commons on December 17, 1940. In answer to the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Sir Kingsley Wood, Mr. Pethick-Lawrence, the hon. member for Edinburgh East had something to say which, it seems to me, indicates clearly what was at the root of the legislation. More than that, it indicates the social and economic movement in the old country. This is what was said on that occasion:
This decision is one which I have felt has very wide ramifications, because in olden days the idea that the community was not responsible in any way for individuals was widely held. It was held with regard to unemployment; it was held with regard to accidents to work people. Gradually we have come to see that we are essentially one another's keepers in these matters, and that we cannot allow people who are injured through circumstances over which they individually have not full control to bear the full burden of their individual losses. The community has, therefore, stepped in. It is stepping in to-day in this matter, and it will have to step in more and more under the complicated system of modern society to meet the immediate dangers to which the individual becomes liable.
Then he went on to deal with the provisions of the war- damage bill which was then under discussion. Under the British act, of course the whole matter of compulsory insurance was considered, and that phase perhaps need not be discussed in dealing with the bill we now have before this house. I should like, however, to point out that it seems to me the present legislation can be regarded only as an initial experiment on the subject.
I can readily understand the difficulties facing the minister in connection with bringing in a measure of this kind, because first of all the question of vulnerable areas comes in. Then there is the question of the difficulty of getting private companies to assume the risks which normally would occur from war-time activity. There is the further difficulty arising from the different forms of warfare this war has brought home to us so emphatically. I think he must in all fairness and all justice consider how this matter has been dealt with in Great Britain. I do not think it is sufficient simply to bring a skeleton bill before this house as he has done and leave so much to regulations.
I was interested in what was said by the hon. member for Victoria, Ontario (Mr. McNevin). In the area from which I come, I suppose that there are more training planes in the sky than in almost any other part of the country, and we are naturally interested in the question of war risk for this type of loss. It is true that up to the present time it has not been substantial. Section 2, the
interpretation section of the bill, has this to say with respect to war risk damage in paragraph (1):
. . . but does not include damage occurring as the result of the restrictions imposed on the display of lights

I assume that this would not cover blackouts.

or of measures taken for training purposes.
I take it that the government has in mind the training of pilots and1 other men in connection with the empire training plan. I think the government should consider the suggestion made by the hon. member for Victoria, Ont., because I believe that many areas in the dominion would be affected.
In connection with war risk premiums we have nothing in the bill to guide us as to what these will be. There is scarcely anything upon which we can base an argument, because this legislation is quite different from that of the United Kingdom, and no comparison or contrast can properly be made.
I would suggest to the minister in charge of this legislation that when the question of war risk premiums comes before the committee he give serious consideration to one particular point, and with this I close my remarks. We have in Canada many men and women who are householders and who are on active service. The homes owned by these people, or the other buildings that they may own, would ordinarily come within the purview of the regulations if, as and when they are made. We should not be picayune with regard to our treatment of these people. I know it is the intention of the government to do the best they can as they see it in their own light, but in many instances I am not sure but that we are treating fairly these men who are serving us on active service. I do not say that with any idea of demagoguery, but I think in this as well as in other matters we should give more consideration to these men. It would not mean much to the country, but it means a tremendous amount to them. If the morale of our fighting,forces is worth anything, it is worth a good deal.
In bringing down any legislation we should be careful to see that the maximum of protection is given to these men. Having regard to the provisions of this bill, I suggest to the minister that in connection with men on active service who normally would be taking out war risk insurance, the premiums should be borne by the dominion government. It seems to me that when men are fighting overseas for us we might make this concession in their favour. I believe it is a right and just charge upon the
War Risk Insurance

taxpayers whom these men are protecting in the fight for righteousness and freedom. I leave this suggestion with the government because I believe it has some merit, merit which goes further than the mere question of saving a few dollars for the treasury of Canada. It means going one step farther and doing something worth while to improve the morale of these men and to provide a proper relationship between the men who are fighting and those of us who are legislating on their behalf.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker the purpose of this bill is to set up a system of insurance of property against war risk and to provide for the payment of compensation for war damage. It was suggested by the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Ross) that the bill might well include insurance against injury to the person, and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) suggested that a separate bill might be introduced for that purpose. I think those suggestions should receive the careful consideration of the government.
The regular insurance companies have refused to issue war risk insurance since the Japs attacked Pearl Harbour, and legislation of this kind becomes necessary.
There are certain definite provisions in this bill. It provides that the owner and occupier of a dwelling house will have his home insured without cost to himself up to an amount not exceeding $3,000. It contains certain provisions for insurance against loss to personal property without cost to the owners of that property. It provides also for indemnity in the case of loss prior to the bill being passed, but only to a limited amount. I take some exception to the limit of $50,000 imposed by the bill upon the payment of damages incurred before the bill becomes law. In my constituency there is a hospital which stands in a prominent place and which provides a vulnerable object for attack. This building cost well over a million dollars and, if it were destroyed prior to the bill becoming law, the damages would be limited to $50,000.
I think the bill should contain a provision to protect a mortgagee, a man who has lent money for the construction of a home. Our ordinary fire insurance policies provide that in such cases loss shall be payable to the mortgagee as his interest may appear, and it seems to me that this bill should contain a provision for the payment of any loss that may be sustained by a mortgagee under these circumstances.
There are certain provisions in this bill, hewever, to which I take serious objection. The bill provides that the rest of the plan

will be established by regulations which will not be made by or apparently approved by the members of this parliament.
The bill provides that regulations will be made as to the manner of making and the forms of the policies, and as to the endorsements on and the applications for the policies.
It provides that regulations shall be made about the premiums to be paid, and about the standard conditions that will be incorporated in the policies; that regulations will be made to authorize insurance companies to execute policies and collect premiums.
In my opinion this system of insurance should not be set up by regulations or by order in council. There is altogether too much government in this country by order in council to-day.
The premiums to be paid, the form of policy, the form of endorsement, the form of application, the terms of the agreements which are to be entered into with the insurance companies-all these should be embodied in the bill or in schedules annexed to it.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) told us when he introduced the resolution that the bill was presented after an exhaustive study had been made from coast to coast. The conclusions of that study should have been embodied, it seems to me, in this bill and should not be left to regulations to be made by civil servants or by an advisory committee that is not responsible to the people of this country. The laws of the dominion should be made in this chamber, with the suggestions, the criticisms and the opposition of the elected members of parliament. We should not delegate our powers to a greater extent than is necessary even in times of war.
We should not let legislative boards or civil servants or advisory committees carry out duties that we were elected to perform, and members of parliament are negligent in their duty to their constituents if they permit the laws of this country to be made by regulations, the terms of which they do not know and have not passed upon or approved. All the provisions of the plan should be inserted in the bill that is submitted to parliament.
If it becomes necessary, as it doubtless may, to make regulations from time to time when parliament is not sitting, such regulations should have force of law only until parliament reassembles and passes and approves them. If parliament does not approve the regulations when it reassembles and they are submitted to it, they should cease to have the force of law.

War Risk Insurance
This bill is contained in eleven printed pages. The War Damages Act of 1941 passed by the parliament of Great Britain for a similar purpose is contained in about ninety-five pages. This bill is shorter, but the regulations passed under it no doubt will be very long. The bill passed by the parliament of Great Britain is long, but the regulations in all probability are short.
I hope that the committee which considers this bill will see to it that it is amended in such a way that all the details of the plan are contained in the bill itself and that the law is not made by regulations about which the members of parliament will have no say.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is one matter which I think should be brought to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) in connection with this bill. I wish to commend him for the purpose and principle of the bill, but I do not think it goes far enough, as perhaps the minister himself would be the first to recognize. It should be broad enough to provide for the protection of all property in the dominion which might be endangered or injured as a result of the war activities in which this country is now engaged. I do not believe that protection of property from war damage should depend entirely on whether or not the owner of the property may have made a contract with the minister. There will be many classes of property in this country which will need to be protected, the owners of which for one reason or another will not have been able to make a contract with the minister in time to protect the property against eventualities which might rush upon us at any moment. I believe there should be something in the bill to take care of situations of that kind. Probably there is, but so far, I have not been able to find it.
The main suggestion I would make to the minister is this. It might be well in a country like Canada to organize this insurance measure in such a way that the provincial governments will cooperate more fully in the organization and administration of the scheme. Already there is at least one province which is going into the insurance of property in rather a big way. I see no reason why each province should not be acting similarly, and I see no reason why cooperation should not be organized between the dominion and provincial governments with the object of accomplishing the aims of this measure.
I intended to comment on the fine spirit of cooperation with the provinces which was manifested in the proposals of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) yesterday with
respect to the youth training and vocational training schemes. I think that is the correct conception of carrying on in this dominion. There has been far too much tendency on the part of a great many people in charge at Ottawa to think that somehow or another they ought to run the show. There is a place for Ottawa to fit in, very definitely; but there is also a place, very definitely, for each of the provincial governments; if the people of Canada get the idea that this country cannot be carried on successfully without centralization, the whole country is headed for trouble. Even in a matter like this insurance bill, the fact should not be lost sight of for a moment that the provincial governments are just as vitally concerned with the property within their borders as is the dominion, and consequently will be just as ready to cooperate and work hard to bring about a set of conditions under which that property will be saved. Then there will be no feeling, on the part of provincial officials at least, that there is a tendency to centralize control at Ottawa. I would suggest to the minister that, if the bill is to be redrafted, he keep in mind this idea of organizing a scheme under which the provinces will cooperate with him and perhaps remove a great deal of the burden from his shoulders, and under which also the provinces will be a great deal happier.

(e) "householder" means an individual occupying and maintaining a self-contained domestic establishment at his own sole expense and maintaining and supporting therein one or more persons connected with him by blood relationship, marriage or adoption.

It is getting late. I did intend to speak, but I am on the banking and commerce committee, and what I have to say I could bring up then. I do wish to say, though, that I feel that this bill is absolutely needed, because neither the minister nor anyone else knows when Canada may have an enemy attack,
War Risk Insurance

and if we do have an attack of that kind there would be a great amount of damage. Therefore, the sooner this bill is put in force, the better for Canada.
There are a few items upon which I wish to remark. I had noted the matter of military aeroplanes used in training; also, in regard to section 2, paragraph (1) (iii), the "proper authority", and also "the carrying out of any attack", that that should include, I imagine, A.R.P. work, because they might do damage, or damage might be done in training, and those things should be covered. That is especially the case when one remembers that bombing planes carry over two thousand incendiary bombs, and it is known that one hundred and thirty-three out of every thousand bombs will cause fires, seventy-five of them being fighting fires, and we have to be prepared. speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my appreciation of the assistance which hon. members have given by their suggestions to-night. I know there are other hon. members who have suggestions to make, but who, from a sense of responsibility and appreciation of the situation, have decided to postpone their remarks until the bill is discussed in the banking and commerce committee. I wish to express my appreciation of their attitude as well.
Although the discussion this evening has not been long, it has taken a fairly wide range; various sections of the bill-definitions and so forth

have been referred to; and I am afraid it will not be possible for me to deal seriatim with the points which have been raised in the debate. On two or three occasions questions were put to me by hon. members opposite and others in the house. I refrained from answering them because under the rules it is not permissible to answer questions in a debate; they can be answered, as I understand it, only by the person who has the floor, upon request; and I should like to say now that I did not intend any discourtesy to any hon. gentleman who asked me questions when I refrained from repl>
ing. I shall try to answer them now if 1 can recollect them.
The leader of the opposition directed attention to a rather important feature of the bill.
If his objection is well founded, it is fundamental-an objection, however, to drafting rather than to principle. It is not intended by section 4 of the bill to empower the minister to establish schemes of insurance which are not authorized by section 3 and other sections

of the bill. That is to say, this is a bill for the establishment of schemes of war risks insurance, not a bill authorizing the establishment of schemes of insurance generally. The leader of the opposition advanced an argument, which appealed to me as ingenious rather than sound, to the effect that the bill as drafted gives a very wide power to the minister to establish schemes of insurance generally. That is not the purpose, nor do I think it is the purport of the bill. Certainly, if there is any danger of the bill being construed in that way it should be amended, and that matter should receive attention in the banking and commerce committee.
The leader of the opposition has made some reference to the deductibility of premiums for income tax and excess profits tax purposes. I thought that, in the explanation of the bill which I gave the committee of the whole when the measure was in the resolution stage, I presented the reasons why it was deemed advisable to provide that these premiums would not be in all cases fully deductible. To put a simple illustration to the house: if the premium is-for the sake of example-15 cents per $100, and one company taking out insurance is in what we call the 79i per cent class under the Excess Profits Tax Act-roughly 80 per cent-that company would really be paying only 3 cents and the government 12 cents of the premium; while a company alongside, a competing company, which was not in that class under the Excess Profits Tax Act, but was paying 40 per cent, would be paying 9 cents out of the 15 cents and the government the other 6 cents. I put that rather briefly and perhaps not too accurately, because in a sense the government is not paying anything, but the government is paying by loss of taxation in both those cases. In the one case, however, the loss of taxation to the government is 12 cents, and in the other case the loss of taxation to the government is 6 cents. It was with a view of equalizing the treatment of those who insure their properties that the provision which is in the bill was inserted there. As I stated to the house, the matter of income tax treatment and excess profits tax treatment of those who insure their properties is a difficult one. There are three tenable positions. One is that the premiums should not be deductible at all, on the ground that they are not incurred as a necessary expense of earning the income but are really expenditures incurred for the preservation of the capital asset. Another is the position taken by the leader of the opposition, that they should be fully deductible, just as fire insurance premiums are fully deductible.
A third is the compromise which I have sug-

War Risk Insurance
gested in the bill before the house. I merely mention that because it was mentioned by the leader of the opposition and because the matter is one of some importance.
Objection has been taken by several hon. gentlemen to the bill on the ground that too much power is given to the governor in council. That position is always taken by oppositions. When this party was in opposition we took the same position repeatedly with regard to measures of the government of that day, and objections to our legislation have repeatedly been put forward on the ground that we leave too much to the governor in council. There is a difference between war-time conditions and peace-time conditions, and I think the argument for leaving a great deal of discretion and power to the governor in council in time of war is very much stronger than in time of peace. In support of that submission I would direct the attention of the house to the fact that the War Measures Act, which was passed I think in 1914 or 1915, substantially in its present form, expressly gave the governor in council power to enter into contracts of insurance of this kind without reference to parliament at all. I should say the war appropriation acts, not the War Measures Act. In a series of war appropriation acts power has always been given the governor in council, among other things, to take a part of the money appropriated by the act for the purposes of promoting the continuance of trade, industry and business communications whether by means of insurance or indemnity against war risk or in any other manner whatsoever; and it would have been strictly within the legal and constitutional powers of the government, not only under the War measures Act but under the War Appropriation Act, to have made provision for this insurance by order in council.
It is because it is a large measure involving an appropriation of $5,000,000 at the outset, and perhaps involving the establishment and carrying on of insurance business of very large dimensions, a measure which certainly concerns parliament as the custodian of the funds provided by the people of Canada, by taxation and loans-it is because of the large and important nature of this measure and because it is a financial measure, that we felt it appropriate to bring it before the House of Commons. I do not feel, however, that we should be asked, either here or in the committee, to spell out every line of the policies which we may see fit to issue or every provision of the schemes which it may be necessary to establish, nor do I think it should be required of us to state what the
rate or rates will be. This business is experimental to a considerable extent, and necessarily a large amount of discretion must be left to the government in establishing such a measure. The insurance of life and insurance against accident to the person as a result of war injury will be provided for by order in council. There are already certain schemes which may be described as insurance schemes. One I think of is a certain measure of insurance to A.R.P. workers. That was provided by order in council. There is in preparation before the treasury board at the present time, although it has come before the board only recently, within the last two or three days, a proposal for compensation to civilians for personal injuries as a result of the war. That is a matter which will be subject probably to change from time to time, and in regard to which amendments must be made. I think it appropriate and entirely in line with the action which has been taken in the past that that should be done by order in council. I am giving that information to the house because, just as I expected, certain members have asked in this debate what we intend to do about protection for civilians from injuries as a result of the war.
Another objection that has been raised tonight to the bill is that in the retroactive section, the section which provides for compensation to those persons who have not taken out policies because there has been no opportunity to take out policies, the limit of $50,000 is too low. An instance was given of a property worth $1,000,000 which might be destroyed before the bill becomes law. The question was asked, what fairness is there in limiting the amount recoverable to $50,000? Naturally we hope and believe that no loss of that magnitude will take place; but if full compensation were to be made in that case, the owner of that property would get the benefit of the assumption that had the bill been law he would have insured his property for the full million dollars, which is aij entirely unjustifiable assumption. The compensation is free, retroactive compensation, and I think it is fair that there should be some limitation of that compensation. Whether $50,000 is the proper amount, I do not know. It is an arbitrary amount and there may be an argument about that feature of it, but certainly there would be no fairness in providing in this bill the same amount of compensation to persons who had not insured, who might never have insured, as there would be to persons who had insured and paid the premium.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: As I read the bill, damage by sabotage is not covered?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: Correct.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: Why not? For example, an enemy agent blows up a war factory, with resulting damage to many people; why are they not covered?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: I do not know that I can answer that very satisfactorily, but I think it is that the matter of sabotage is very hard to determine. I think it would result in endless debate as to whether the damage really was due to sabotage or some other cause, I believe that is the main reason for not putting it in. The kind of damage insured against here is damage the cause of which is readily ascertainable; it is there for every one to see. There may be other reasons as well, but that is what occurs to me at the moment.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: Of course by ruling out sabotage you give the person who suffers the damage no chance at all. Would it not be more fair if he were left in the position that if he could prove the damage was caused by sabotage, he would be covered?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: I think, for example, riot and civil commotion can be covered without any difficulty. I understand that the one purpose of this bill is to give coverage that cannot be obtained in any other way at the present time to anyone who wants to insure. That, I understand, is the principle.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PROVISION FOR COMPENSATION FOR WAR DAMAGE TO PROPERTY
speechtext: Yes; that is correct, to give coverage against damage from war risks which cannot be obtained from the insurance companies. I do not know whether sabotage can or cannot be covered, and there may be other reasons in that case. I think there are.
